speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are
68108-15?
called I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has the minister, or I suppose I should say the government, considered advising the wheat board to permit individual farmers to market grain in excess of marketing quota where such excess grain is donated to the national fund for European flood relief?
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of the question has been carefully considered by the wheat board and by the government. I think I can do no better than to read a letter that I directed to Mr. Probe, who is the chairman of the Saskatchewan committee for European flood relief, It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Probe:
I have your telegram ol February 21st with reference to contributions to the European flood relief fund.
Even though your objectives are so worthy, I am afraid that it is not possible for the Canadian wheat board to authorize deliveries above the established quota for the plan you have in mind. You will appreciate, I am sure, that the purpose of the delivery quota system is to provide maximum delivery opportunities to all producers. The board is exerting every effort to permit the highest possible quota at each delivery point. To the extent that deliveries in excess of quotas were permitted, it would mean that other producers would be unable to deliver up to their own quotas.
Many requests of this nature, for delivery of grain over and above the quota, are received. In most cases, the objectives are very worthy- churches, charitable drives, etc. In each case, however, it has been necessary to advise that, due to the necessity of providing maximum delivery opportunities to all producers, the request could not be met.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF MALTREATMENT AWARDS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's notice sent to the Minister of National Defence as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs has just been sent over to me. This is not *a matter to be handled by the Department of External Affairs; it is a decision that will have to be made by the government. The government appointed, as the hon. gentleman knows, the chief justice of his own province to examine the question of the rules that should apply to the distribution of the funds held by the custodian of enemy property, which are insufficient to cover all the claims that could legitimately be made against that fund.
The chief justice of Nova Scotia, as a royal commissioner, made a very careful study of the whole situation, and submitted a report, which in general was accepted by the government, with some slight modifications that were discussed with the commissioner after he had submitted his report to iron out some little difficulties in administration.
That report provided that it would be assumed that all prisoners of war in the hands of the Japanese did suffer maltreatment and should get an award on the basis of one dollar for each day of internment, and that with respect to other prisoners there would not be a general assumption that they had been subjected to maltreatment beyond the usages of warfare between civilized nations, but that any who had been subjected to maltreatment could make a special claim and their claim would be considered by the claims commissioner.
Representations have been made that the presumption that all prisoners were subjected to maltreatment should extend to the prisoners held by the axis powers, by the Germans or the Italians. No decision has yet been made by the government to depart from the recommendations of the commissioner. Representations have been made that we should do so and I understand that further representations by an organized group of war prisoners are expected to be made. That is the present position. There has been rfo decision to depart from the recommendations of the commissioner, but representations have been received and further representations are expected.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 26, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate some hon. members of the opposition have attempted to label this budget a rich man's budget, as a budget which does precious little for the small man, or as a budget which is doing very little for the little fellow. In their endeavour to establish this point they laid great emphasis on the personal income tax, and attempted to establish that the so-called little fellow gets only a very small reduction. As an example they lay stress on the married man with two children, having an income of $2,400, who gets a small reduction. I think they could have emphasized further that this same man with an income of $2,400 will pay a tax of only $15. They could have gone farther, if they wished to be fair, and emphasized that this same man with a wife and two children and an income of $2,300, will not have to pay any income tax at all.
Let us take a man with a wife and two children and an income of $3,000. He is drawing family allowances. His income tax on $3,000 would be $105, yet he receives from the federal government by way of family allowances an amount of approximately $150 for the year. In fact the so-called little man gets a bonus, if you want to put it that way, from the government of some $45 for that year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not the government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From the dominion government or the people of Canada. I am trying to point out that the so-called little man is not being left out in the cold; and the same applies to the man with an income of $2,400. He pays a tax of $15, and he gets from the federal government approximately 68108-1574
The Budget-Mr. Decore $150. Thereby he is receiving a bonus of $135 on top of the income of $2,400.
Furthermore I am sure that every hon. member in the house has personal knowledge of young married couples, with two children, who have also in their care their fathers or mothers who may have reached ages of 65 or 70 years. These young married people perhaps do not have a legal obligation to look after their fathers and mothers in their declining years, but 'they certainly have a moral obligation.
Again, under our system of government, as we have it, these old people are receiving assistance and, at the same time, the young people in the lower income brackets are receiving an indirect benefit. But let us not forget that the government is spending this year for purposes of social security, such as family allowances, old age pensions and social security in other forms the sum of approximately one billion dollars.
This legislation dealing with social services was intended for and was designed to assist the so-called little fellow. Let us, for example, consider family allowances. The purpose of that legislation was to help those people who are in the lower income brackets, to assist them in buying food, clothing and school books for their children, so that those children, who eventually will take our plapes in our national life, may receive that degree of help. And so one can talk almost indefinitely about the assistance this government is giving to people in the lower income tax brackets.
I wonder if there is any member in the house who would rise in his place and say that we in Canada have not the best form of social services in the whole world. And may I say further that when reference is made to the so-called little man or little fellow, the small man, I take objection to these terms. In my view it sounds more like the sort of thing the Russians were and still are teaching in Soviet Russia. Those expressions remind me very much of what we heard in Alberta when people were talking about the fifty big shots who were running Canada. In my view that is the wrong kind of psychology being applied by some politicians in classifying the people of this country.
I do not know whether one ought to judge a person by the size of his pocketbook; but in my opinion the so-called little fellow is just as big and probably in some respects bigger than the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) who used this term. On the other hand, the so-called big shots could be just as small as the smallest of the so-called little fellows. The use of these terms should be avoided, because it is a clear case

The Budget-Mr. Decore of discrimination when we refer to big shots and little shots, big fellows and little fellows, big fry and small fry. That kind of classification is not only undesirable but also detrimental to our Canadian way of life.
Returning to the question of the personal income tax, let us examine whether we have before us a rich man's budget. Again I refer to the married man with two children who are eligible for payments under the Family Allowances Act. Let us consider the case of the man who has an income of $50,000 a year, and see what happens to him under this budget. One sees at once that he would be required to pay an income tax of $21,099. Is that a rich man's budget?
Let us go farther. Supposing the man with two dependents is fortunate or unfortunate enough to make an income of $200,000 a year. How much does he have to pay in taxation? Under this budget, out of his $200,000 he will have to turn over to "Doug" Abbott-I mean to the Minister of Finance- the sum of $125,504.
Is this a rich man's budget? Does not part of the $125,000 this man pays as income tax go by way of a contribution to our billion-dollar social welfare program, in order to help out the man in the lower income brackets, by way of family allowances, old age pensions, and other forms of social security?
The other day the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance spoke in the debate-and, incidentally, I thought he made a valuable contribution to it. I turn to his speech, as it is reported at page 2394 of Hansard, and I challenge any hon. member in the opposition, or any other member in the house, to disprove these words of the parliamentary assistant:
We must not forget that In spite of all we have had to do in all fields, in spite of all that we have done, our rates of income tax here in Canada are the lowest in the world and our exemptions are the highest in the world. That is true in spite of the fact that the government here in Canada has one of the best systems of social security in the world; in spite of the fact that we have the best system of old age security in the world today; in spite of the fact that we are looking, through social security, after the small people of this country-because, contrary to what has been said on the other side, we are making transfer payments to those who are in need.
This stands as a challenge to any hon. member who believes he can prove the contrary.
And what about our corporations? Sometimes people seem to like to refer to corporations as sinister bodies organized for the purpose of robbing the poor, and the sole purpose of which is to prevent the so-called little fellow from taking his proper place in
[Mr. Decore.1
the world. Let us examine how much income tax these corporations have to pay and, for the purposes of our investigation, we will take the round figure of a million dollars. The corporation with a net income of $1 million is required to pay back to the people of Canada, under this budget, nearly half of that by way of income tax. Not only do these corporations provide jobs for millions of people in this country, but it is also very desirable in a young nation like ours to have groups of men getting together in common ventures for the development of the resources of our country and the creation of jobs for our people.
I am a great believer in free enterprise. I am a great believer that every man in this country should be free to take risks, to use his initiative in order to better conditions, not only for himself but for his community and country. Canada is a young nation with tremendous resources, some of which have already been tapped. Year by year we are pushing back the frontiers. My grandfather came to this country with a pioneering spirit, a spirit of free enterprise, and so did all our pioneers. In fact, the development of Canada would never have been possible had it not been for the pioneering spirit of those who came here in the years gone by, to settle not only in the west but in other provinces of this great country. They had that spirit of free enterprise which has made it possible for Canada to go ahead as she has.
We have had many ministers of finance in this country. Some of them were truly great, but I think history will record that one of the greatest was our present Minister of Finance. In spite of our gigantic social security measures and our gigantic defence preparations, since the last war Canada has been able to reduce her national debt, a debt incurred because of two previous wars, to the extent of some $2,500 million, thus saving the people of Canada $63 million each and every year in interest charges.
Referring to the national debt, the hon. member for Peace River had this to say, and I quote from page 2367 of Hansard of February 24 as follows:
While the minister revelled in what he called a spectacular federal debt reduction, he said nothing at all about the increase in the gross holdings by foreigners of Canadian assets.
And again:
The net amount of those assets, held mainly by Americans, is no less than $5,800 million. They constitute a foreign debt owed by the people of Canada collectively, and in every way they serve to drain out of our country very large quantities of goods to pay the interest and dividends.

Does the hon. member not realize that most of that United States capital went to his own province of Alberta? That was not due to the policy of this government, it was due to the policy of the provincial government which has jurisdiction over natural resources in the province. I have said it before and I repeat that since the discovery of the Leduc field from 75 per cent to 90 per cent of the proven oil reserves in the province are now in the hands of United States corporations.
Many challenges are thrown out on the floor of the house by the hon. member for Peace River about the type of government they have in Alberta. Not so long ago he challenged the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who incidentally accepted the challenge, and since then the hon. member for Peace River has been walking in a daze. Just to indicate some of the things he has said, I refer again to another statement he made, as reported on page 2368 of Hansard:
There is another question that we have to face. That prospect in my judgment is very real as a consequence of the shortsightedness of this government in matters of trade and finance. We should have been promoting trade with the United Kingdom and other sterling countries with all our energy, on a barter basis if necessary, in order to avoid the dangers we now face as a consequence of running up these serious adverse trade balances with the United States.
That is what the hon. member said on the floor of this house. But not so long ago the hon. member addressed the Rotary Club in Montreal, and I quote from the Gazette of February 11, 1953, as follows:
He said it was unthinkable to suggest Canada could compete successfully on the open markets of the world.
Free trade is a myth. There is nothing we produce in Canada today that is not protected in some fashion.
Mr. Low declared Canada was now at the crossroads of conflicting views. He asked what course the country should follow.
Shall we talk foolishly about free trade and thereby induce action that will destroy thriving industries and occupations that contribute to the strength and vitality of our nation?
Or shall we adopt a policy of careful conservation of our resources that will make our country great?
If ever there were conflicting views, not in the minds of the Canadian people but in the mind of one man, this is an example. It looks to me like a case of split personality and I am reminded of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.
Let me turn now to the budget. Our total expenditures under this budget amount to $4,750 million. Of that total, $2,000 million will go for national defence; $450 million will be paid out as interest on the national debt created by the last two wars; and $1,000
The Budget-Mr. Decore million will be paid out in the form of social security payments to which I have already referred. In other words, nearly three-quarters of our total expenditures will be used, first, for maintaining our security from outside aggression and, second, for maintaining our national security. The keystone to the greatness of Canada is her ability to look after the welfare of her own people and to defend herself against outside aggression.
This budget indicates that not only have we been able to bring about a tax reduction, but the dangers of inflation have been lessened and at present they are not as real as they were before. I think this is due to our record production. As a westerner coming from Alberta, one of the three prairie provinces, I should like to point out the contribution which those provinces have made to the national production. Of course, I am talking about wheat.
Sometimes we who come from western Canada are accused of talking too much about wheat. But we must not forget that agriculture is not only the basic industry of Canada, it is the most important industry in the west. Our most important agricultural product is wheat. In 1952, our last crop year, the farmers of the three prairie provinces produced 668 million bushels of wheat, an achievement which has never been equalled before. This was the largest crop in the history of Canada. Of that total wheat production, 96J per cent was produced by the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
That was the achievement of only a handful of farmers. There are only 231,000 farmers in the three prairie provinces, whereas the statistics indicate that there are 5 [DOT] 5 million farmers in the United States, or twenty times as many. Yet the volume of wheat produced by Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba was approximately one-half of the entire wheat production in the United States. Let me put it to you differently. The farmers of western Canada produced a volume of wheat equal to 66 per cent of the total production of Soviet Russia which includes the Ukraine, known as the grain basket of Europe. Still differently, we in western Canada produced 40 per cent of the average production of the entire continent of Europe in pre-war years. Still differently, we produced 285 million bushels more than the entire production of Australia and Argentina combined in recent years. You can readily see that agriculture is not only Canada's basic industry but also her most important industry, and wheat one of our most important products.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
I hope that the negotiations which are now going on in Washington between the importing and the exporting countries of the world for the renewal of the international wheat agreement will be successfully concluded. In view of the high cost of production and especially the high cost of machinery, I do feel that the price we should get for our Canadian wheat should be more than $1.80 per bushel.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with those who have extended their sympathy to the family of the former deputy minister of finance, the late Dr. Clark, and to those in the department with whom he was associated. I know that, while some may have differed with some of his financial philosophy, he has nevertheless left a mark of respect and of the dignity of his office, and he will live in the memory of his family and those who were his friends.
I realize that the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Decore) has emphasized some features in the budget that are important. I hope he will not assume that it is any reflection on the type of argument he put forward if I do not follow his remarks as closely as he might expect. I realize and appreciate with him that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. I sometimes wonder if it has not been somewhat forgotten by those who have been emphasizing our progress and prosperity in other respects. I observed that the hon. member differed considerably with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who so ably demonstrated exactly what this budget means in dollars and cents. I am not going to question either the correctness of his speech or his reference to the effect that the man with a low income was saving a lot more in taxes than the hon. member for Greenwood said.
I believe the hon. member for Greenwood said that a man with a salary of $2,400 would save $1. The hon. member for Vegreville said that the hon>. member for Greenwood was away out in his figures because a man receiving that salary would actually save $3. So there is quite a difference. It is three times as much as the hon. member for Greenwood said; but, because of the effect of inflation on the value of the dollar, if he saves $3 it will only buy about half as much as the same amount would have bought ten or fifteen years ago.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, I wonder if my hon. friend listened to my speech. I never mentioned anything about $3.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the hon. member did not but I followed what he said. I listened very carefully. In fact I could not help but
EMr. Decore.]

hear him. The hon. member for Vegreville said that he would pay $15 instead of $18.
I think my arithmetic is still right and that the difference would be $3. The hon. member for Greenwood said he would pay $18 instead of $19. I wonder which is true, so I hope that they will check their figures, because if either man is wrong I think we should let the public know. As I say, I am not going to indulge in argument because this is much more than a $3 proposition. This is the most gigantic budget that has ever been presented to the house. Whether it is $1 less than last year or $3 less than last year, it is taking on the average, visibly and invisibly, directly and indirectly, approximately $1,700 for every family of five in Canada.
Why, Mr. Speaker, never in our history has anything nearly approached the size to which government business has grown in this country. It is certainly the biggest business we have in Canada. We have a population of some 14 million people, and I doubt whether any similar number of people in the world have ever been called upon to raise the tremendous amount of money that is involved in this budget of almost $4| billion.
We have heard a great deal about prosperity, and I realize that we have a degree of prosperity. Some have called it a false or artificial prosperity. Others say: Well, it is prosperity anyway. But to say the least, by the very nature of this prosperity it must appear to you, sir, and to every hon. member in the house and the taxpayers of Canada, that it is at least an inflationary type of prosperity. It is built up chiefly on the greatest enterprise in Canada, the government's inflationary spending policy. One would almost imagine that the government was trying to spend itself into prosperity. It seems to me that they think that the more they spend the more prosperous the country is going to be.
Of course, as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said so ably yesterday, if we had an election every year we might get some of this $1 or $3 relief for those who are termed the small taxpayers, because it seems to be only at election time that any thought of tax reduction has even been intimated. In 1949 and again on the eve of an election now the government has done the same thing. They are not giving quite as much tax relief on the eve of this election as on the eve of the last one, and they are only making it effective for half a year. It makes one wonder after all, with all the guesses and anticipation reported around the capital, whether or not we are going to have an

election this year. I think that the government members are as doubtful about that as they are about everything else. I think they said:	In case we do not have an
election we will not risk the whole thing this year; we will just give half of the reductions this year and then we will have the rest for next year. We will save something for another session. If we do not go to the people until next year, and if our popularity slips as much as it has in the past year, then we will give them a real gunshot prescription next year for an election in 1954.
I know that it has been called an election budget, and it has been called a sunset budget; but I see very little relief in it for the great mass of taxpayers, 75 per cent of our people. I have mentioned the government's spending policy, and I believe that is what it is. We are to spend $2 4 billion for defence, and I often wonder what would happen if there were no fear of war to impose such an obligation on this young country. I often wonder what would happen if such an occasion should arise because the government is spending enormous sums of money on a cost-plus basis and I have seen no signs at all of any economy. This so-called prosperity is bolstered by cost-plus contracts, subsidies, bonuses, pensions and so forth. We have never seen such a lavish distribution of such a huge amount of taxes taken from the people of the country.
I have mentioned that very little economy is shown by the government. When you pause and consider, Mr. Speaker, the complacency and extravagance, the irregularities and thefts by individuals-some call it petty theft but the government, I believe, calls it normal theft; some other minister I believe called it just theft as usual where there is a lot of money being handed around-you would think this government, these tired old incumbents who have been in office too long, would not so disregard money. But they have said:	What is a
million dollars? The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said not long ago when the Leader of the Opposition had shown him how to save a lot of money:	Why, if all of these
proposals you have made were put into effect we would not save more than $100 million.
After all, surely, Mr. Speaker, we have good resources but not so great that we can say that $100 million does not mean very much. Surely the people paying taxes in this dominion, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) said, have a right to some consideration. The total national revenue of this dominion is enormous at present, coming from industries that give employment to people and who pay about 50
The Budget-Mr. Rowe per cent of their earnings in taxes. Savings in private income taxes are infinitesimal compared with the taxes paid in other ways-by the man who buys an automobile, by the man who buys boots and shoes for the baby, by the man who buys clothes and many lines of foodstuffs-I refer especially to sales tax. It is amusing to me because I can remember how these great champions of the Liberal party almost wept crocodile tears when the sales tax was put up to 6 per cent. I remember the late prime minister saying that we should not have any sales tax at all, but then he got to like it and almost doubled it before he retired.
Many departments in the government seem to be running almost by themselves and we have had all sorts of rumours about camps here and camps there and $24 billion of the taxpayers' money being spent for goods that were being destroyed and wasted. We only have one little peek at about 1 per cent of that whole expenditure-because we finally stirred the government to have an investigation made. As a member on this side has just said, there is a great difference in the bookkeeping. One report said there was no bookkeeping at all and the Auditor General said they had at least eight different kinds of bookkeeping, none of them sound.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, it is not a joke when you see departments acting almost as though they were endeavouring to see how much money they could spend-whether it is on nylon stockings, silk petticoats, bedroom slippers, cement stolen or cement that is not needed or, as someone else has said, fish ponds for fire protection. We have all sorts of signs, as I have said, of irregularities, extravagance, and reckless disregard for money and, yes, even theft itself. It is to be expected, when a government is in power for a long time, for almost a third of a century with the exception of four or five years. This government seem to think they are the greatest legislators that this country has ever had. They say what is $1 million? What is $100 million? We can spend our way into power; we can get ourselves popular and pull ourselves up by our bootlaces and it doesn't matter what we spend.
In 1939, for instance, printing and stationery costs of this government were about $1 million. This past year they were $13 million. The figure for film broadcasting, advertising, radio broadcasting- generally advertising the political wares of the government with the people's money-is up from $600,000 in 1939 to $7 million. Then, of course, Mr. Speaker, it is generally recognized now that members of this government are the greatest travellers we

The Budget-Mr. Rowe have had since confederation. They go all over the world and they go in great groups. They take fellowship tours to South American countries, Europe, and all over the world. They come back and tell us what great trips they have had and we, certainly as taxpayers, hope that they have enjoyed themselves, because I notice that in 1939 travelling and transportation cost the government of this country $4 million. Last year it cost $53 million.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have telephones and telegraph expenses-telephoning back to each other to find out how the situation is in the different ridings, how the C.C.F are doing in Saskatchewan, perhaps whether the Social Crediters are making any more gains in British Columbia, and so forth. In 1939 those telegrams, telephone calls and stamps cost about $1 million. Last year they cost $13 million.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these things get out of hand and that is what happened across the border in the United States. When Sarnoff was asked to investigate expenditure for defence in the United States recently he found that the government over there, which the American people thought had been in too long-and in fact thought about the same of them as our electors are now thinking of this government in Canada-had been extravagant. That government was defeated, and one of the reasons was that when Sarnoff reported he said there was so much plush and extravagance in their expenditures that he was sure that with any kind of caution at all they could be cut by at least 10 per cent.
Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, if our expenditures could be cut by 10 per cent. It would certainly pay the taxpayers of Canada to change their board of directors. As I say, we have had an investigation on only 1 per cent of the picture. We do not know whether we could save 10 per cent on expenditures or not, but the rumours we have heard indicate callous extravagance and irregularities which have not been investigated in other departments. There is no use mentioning it here because this government will not believe what they already have found-let alone look for more. They are sorry they even looked as far as they did.
Every sincere businessman in this country is concerned about how this enormous tax burden is being spent. I say with all sincerity that there has never been such a demonstration of laxity, carelessness and negligence in departmental administration as we have seen. I am forced by rumours that I have heard, and by the evidence I see of this type of expenditure, to conclude that the


department that has been investigated is probably not much worse than any other department. I hope that this government during the coming summer, and in the twilight of their long term, will at least become cost-conscious. I know that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is in a great minority today in the house, but he will certainly do his best, surely, when he thinks of the tremendous recklessness that has been demonstrated in the past, to try, at least in the last few months this government expects to be in office, to save some of the taxpayers' money so that the situation will not grow worse as the year goes on. Millions of dollars have been wasted and millions of dollars have been spent on architects and engineering services on cost-plus contracts. It almost appears a case of the more the cost the more the tax will be. At Wain-wright, Alberta, they spent $22,000 for a swimming pool. They spent $280,000 for two gymnasiums; and $54,000 for bowling alleys. Crown Assets Disposal Corporation sells airplane hangars for $6,300, and in Newfoundland the defence department spends $283,700 just for dismantling-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On many occasions I have mentioned the importance of the great basic industry of agriculture. I cannot help being in agreement with the hon. member for Vegreville in that regard when he says that

agriculture is basic. There is nothing more important to the life and economy of the country or no enterprise more indigenous to the whole economy-yes, of our very life- than is agriculture. It does not matter how many men get rich in it. It is not a matter of how much money they roll up or put in the banks or in investments. It is the life of our people. It is important in time of peace, and it is fundamental in time of war, that we keep a healthy agriculture. I know that truth has been felt in this country since the days of confederation. It has been felt across the border by the great statesmen in the United States all down through the years. It is a matter which is not even debatable because every hon. member in this house, no matter to what party he belongs, recognizes it as a fact.
President Lincoln of the United States once said that any government which failed to recognize agriculture, by allowing any other industry to conflict with its progress, was certainly sacrificing the very integrity of the nation. If that was true then, Mr. Speaker, it is certainly doubly true today because the population of the world is so much greater than it was at that time. When millions of our brothers and sisters in Europe and all over the world are starving to death this very minute for want of food; when we have a world organization trying to develop food production; and when we have the fear of war to the extent that we are spending these huge sums of money to prepare for our defence, surely there is no one within the sound of my voice who does not believe that it is just as important now to keep agriculture on a sound and permanent basis.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help thinking that it has often been forgotten that the farmer holds a unique place in our economy. He is not only a producer of the essentials for our very livelihood but he is a capitalist and a labour man all in one. He is running a corporation that needs more skill every day than it did in the years that are past. He must provide his working capital. He must keep his machinery and efficiency up to standard so that he can produce economically, or he goes out of business, because it is a fairly marginal business that he is in. His costs are rising and his prices are falling. He is certainly disturbed as to what is going to happen. His income must maintain his family and educate them. Today, with the high price of automobiles and machinery the high level of municipal taxes and so on, the burden is more complex than ever before. His return from his investment and his labour is the lowest-in percentage gain on capital investment-of any industry in Canada. He therefore travels on a small 68108-158
The Budget-Mr. Rowe margin. His hourly rate of wages is away below normal. Even though he is paying his hired man, usually, almost five times as much as he did ten years ago, even so that hired man is getting less money than is his brother who is working in manufacturing plants, and certainly much less than the government is paying in government employment in the neighbouring districts. Statistics show that over the last twenty years Canadian farmers as a whole, if they had taken the same money for themselves and their wives as they pay to their hired men and hired girls, would have made no money on their capital investment. The current outlook is not good, Mr. Speaker. Farm prices are declining rapidly. No one who is watching the economy of this country can be unaware of that fact. No one can appreciate the complexity of the problem as well as can those who have been engaged in the industry and who are familiar with farmers generally.
I believe Mr. Hannam of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said:
For those who have the erroneous impression that farmers have been enjoying unprecedented prosperity, it would be well to re-state the fact that the farmer's income depends not on prices alone but on farm prices in relation to farm costs. In recent years farm costs have risen more than have farm prices. Based on price relationship, the farmer's purchasing power if represented by the index of 100 in 1948 has been less every year since.
He goes on to show-and these are facts1- that the farmers income is down about 18 per cent since 1948, that it has gone down a great deal during the last eighteen months, and is likely to be down, over 20 per cent before the end of this year.
I feel that the government is somewhat more responsible now probably than in normal times because during the last ten years they have developed a monopolistic control of the farmer's business and they have almost made it look as though they were heading agriculture toward a socialized industry. A number of years ago this parliament enacted a farm prices support act. What has been done about floor prices? They change from day to day, from week to week, from month to month and from year to year. It depends on what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seems to have had for his breakfast as to what you are going to get for bacon, eggs and other products. I believe the Minister of Agriculture told us here a short time ago that there was absolutely no shortage of butter and that there would not be for a long time. But two days afterwards he takes the freeze off the butter and lets a supply go out.
2472	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Rowe
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we should have some rationalization of this policy. Whether it is a sound policy for agriculture or whether it is the right way to approach this unique problem of agriculture in our country is not now my problem but at least it should be rationalized so that the producer would be protected against the terrific changes, dependent upon the mood of the Minister of Agriculture or on how he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) are getting along.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian farm prices have been declining so much that we are already in a recession if not almost in a depression. For instance, our prices have dropped, as I have mentioned, about 18 per cent in the last two years. Between July of 1951 and December of 1952 the weekly wages in industry manufacturing products which the farmer buys have gone up by 12 per cent. There have been some declines in other industrial prices; some I believe have probably fallen slightly. I believe prices of building materials have fallen about 2 per cent; prices of iron and steel products are up 5 per cent.
The decline in many of these important farm prices is much more than the 18 per cent to which I have referred. To take a few examples, I would mention livestock, poultry and eggs-animal products, you might call them. In the last year and a half those products have dropped in price between 25 per cent and 30 per cent. In the same time the costs of the farmer in operating his farm have gone up by 35 per cent. They have gone up about 35 per cent during the last two years. The government surely could not have taken this fact into account, because they have added another 15 per cent on the rubber tires that the farmer uses on his implements. If there ever was a man forgotten by this government it is the farmer. This government seldom have forgotten the voters but they have certainly forgotten the farmer in this budget. The government have lost his markets; have increased his costs; have monopolized his business; have cost him millions of dollars in wheat trading, and have lost his animal products markets. The government say: That is not our fault. Nothing seems to be their fault when the thing is going well. When the goose hangs high, of course, it is all to their credit. But when prices begin to fall, then it is somebody else's fault, not theirs. It seems reasonable that a government which has elected to follow this type of policy should take some responsibility for the results. It is not enough merely to say that it has not been successful, or to give other reasons. We have urged from this side of the house on scores of occasions that the government should have
IMr. Rowe.]

encouraged the calling of a commonwealth conference on trade before they did. When it was called they reluctantly took part in that conference. We have urged that something should be done; that conferences and meetings should be called at which convertibility of exchange could be discussed and finally brought about.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture have been very much alarmed. When they are alarmed at this government it is certainly time to stop, look and listen, because they are usually very courteous to the government. They now see the danger signs, and they are urging the government to bring out some policy. I quote from one of their meetings, as follows:
Return to convertibility of sterling and dollar currencies.
Removal of restrictions on dairy products moving into the U.S.
Establishment by nation-members within the United Nations' food and agriculture organization of an international program to handle surpluses.
They are wondering how they will get rid of their surpluses; they are fearful about the fact that the livestock market in Britain is lost entirely, and that the United States, in spite of the Geneva pact, refuses to take our cheese. They are conscious of the fact that we have imported into this country substantial quantities of cheese, beef and poultry products as well as pork products, canned and otherwise, even though we have lost the markets for our own products overseas.
The record of this government in dealing with the farmers' problems is one of bungling, misrepresentation, misjudgment, guesswork; and it now looks like a patchwork quilt as you look back upon it. We have told the Minister of Agriculture and the government during the last two or three years that they were losing hundreds of millions of dollars for the western wheat grower. It is now a matter of historical fact that hundreds of millions of dollars more could have been received for their wheat when the deals were made. The fact is that the government does not seem to know now what to ask for the wheat under the new international wheat agreement. I see that the United States are talking about asking $2.50 a bushel. The government has thought they needed a little more than $1.80. Now they suggest they should have $2.20 or $2.25. On another occasion they said they might take $2.15. Later on they thought they would get $2.10. It sounds like an auctioneer in a farm barnyard trying to sell a product. Whether it is the right system or not I am not going to argue. But this strange type of bargaining, underselling our wheat at $1.50 under world

prices at times and now dickering on an international wheat agreement and considering selling it at 60 cents to 70 cents below world prices, is hard to understand. It is very difficult for the farmer to know where he is. I am more directly concerned with the dangerous spectacle confronting the dairy farmers of this country and the beef producers; in other words, the mixed farmers from coast to coast. I think that the farmers might have had a better deal. Those who are using a lot of machinery and have big production, as have the western farmers in recent years, are not in as bad a plight as some of the other farmers. But there is not a member within the sound of my voice who knows anything about farming communities in either Ontario or Quebec who does not know that every dairyman and every livestock producer in Canada is worried sick these days. They are wondering what is going to happen. They know the government has oleomargarined the dairy industry. They know that you have made the pork industry so uncertain that the farmers do not know whether to keep more hogs or fewer. They know that this government paid 69 cents a pound for bacon, stored it and then sold it at 47 cents a pound. Somebody said 32 cents.

speechtext: I would not be surprised at what they sold it for because, Mr. Speaker, if any business was run like that the management would be fired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are going to be.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If any big business was managed in the way that this government has managed the biggest business in this nation, regarding markets and the government spending, why they could not face their shareholders. That is why I suppose they are wondering when they should face them; but the day of reckoning is coming fast. Their record consists of errors, bungling and miscalculation. If their guesswork is no better about election day then it has been with regard to Canada's economy, then I do not pay much attention to those who pound their desks and make loud noises when some of their colleagues get up to speak, and say, We had a big majority last time and we shall have it again. That does not sink in very well when you realize what is happening in this country. I do not know whether any member of this government knows, because there are a lot of things they do not know, that conditions will get better or worse during the year. Certainly if they get worse I would say to the few ministers who are left in the house: Beware of the rumbling in the mulberry 68108-158i
The Budget-Mr. Rowe bushes. You had better think twice. You might get one more year in office, one more year in power, if you consider that discretion is the better part of valour and do not go to the country until next year, because your days are now numbered.
In the ten years from 1941 to 1951 Canada's farm population, according to the recent census, was reduced by 10 per cent. I know that many farmers will say the answer to that is the big combine and the improved farm machinery. We have had farm machinery for quite a while. True it has increased somewhat in recent years. You who come from the bountiful wheat fields of western Canada can produce more with the same machinery and the same amount of help than you could years ago; but in eastern Canada, in Ontario and Quebec on mixed farms, it helps a little but not a great deal. I do not know that you can milk ten cows any faster in 1952 than you could in 1942 with the same machines. We had milking machines then. I have done a little of that, but perhaps not as much as some of the people have. I do not think you can clean the cow stables out much quicker with the same kind of litter carrier and the same kind of manure fork than you could ten years ago. With regard to the help on the farms in Ontario and Quebec, I think the livestock farms are employing just about the same number of men as they were before. But what about Canada's population over-all? The population of the cities and towns in Canada has grown by 32 per cent in that time.
What is the government trying to do about trade, Mr. Speaker? So far as agricultural trade is concerned, they have done absolutely nothing. They have done less than nothing so far as British trade is concerned. They did not even try to hold the British market. They lost it just as rapidly and just as completely as the same party lost it between 1921 and 1930. I was in this house at that time. If I made the same speech now that I made in 1928 it would fit the picture almost perfectly, because in 1921, when this party came into power, we had an enormous market in Britain. We sold 255 million pounds of bacon and more cheese than we had sold any time in the previous hundred years.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the price? What was the price in 1921?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not analogous at all. We sold more cheese in 1921 than now. We sold over 100 million pounds of cheese away back in 1900. The British market has been the best market for agricultural products of any place in the world over the last seventy-five years. I want to say to my hon. friends from western Canada-I know they

The Budget-Mr. Rowe will agree with me, or at least most of them will-that we have lost our market for dairy products, cheese and animal products. I am getting very tired, and I have been tired for a long time, of this looking to the north and south for agricultural markets. I am not going to argue-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about prices in 1930?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend does not know that the prices are higher now than they were in 1930 I am surprised that he is even here. Mr. Speaker, I know that many people do not like to hear all these things. But it is a good thing for some people who have not been here long to know that history does repeat itself.
Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us about that delightful trip he made, and he told us that certain men made the trip with him. They were all good fellows, and so is he. The South American people could not help liking the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We all like him here, personally. But I never heard him mention agriculture once.
He was down there looking for markets for industrial production, looking for markets that we might have for automobiles, and things like that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about wheat?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, we sold wheat before there, too. But what about butter and eggs? His viewpoint, that we have to look north and south for trade, is just the same as their party's viewpoint was before the turn of the century. His party lost an election in which they wanted commercial union with the United States, and they have been looking north and south ever since. This Conservative party sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker-[DOT] and which will likely be sitting to your right after the next election-has consistently said that we must have markets in Europe, and in other places that need our food. Does anyone think that Argentina will buy beef from Canada? Does anyone think that Texas will buy beef from Canada? Do you think they will send our farm products down to a country where they milk a thousand cows on one farm, but do not need a barn.
I visited one place in the southern United States where they milk a thousand cows, but they did not even have to have any frost-proofing-nothing but a shelter to keep the rain off their cows. They are out, the whole year round.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian agriculture is unique in that regard. Canadian agriculture is carried on in a cold and frigid country. But


we should remember agriculture is part of our great wealth. But our climatic conditions are not as favourable as they are in tropical areas.
However, Mr. Speaker, I do hope that the government will give some thought to restoring these markets, which are natural markets for Canada. I have made reference to our increased costs'-and I see that the time at my disposal is rapidly running out. I am not going to delay the house unduly, but with the few minutes I have left I shall not place on record further figures dealing with increased costs and lower prices. These are figures anyone can read, and I shall leave them with hon. members.
The government has done very little, if anything at all, to help the farmer who is engaged in mixed farming. They have done very little for the livestock producer or the dairy producer to retain the markets that we had. And when we are in that position, I ask the government to be very careful when they import, as they are doing today, 14 million pounds of beef, 5 million pounds of pork, 2i million pounds of poultry products and 10 million pounds of cheese. We are exporting very little, if any, cheese. 1 ask the government to be very careful about these importations, especially at a time when these export markets are slipping from us.
It seems to me the only evidence of concern shown by the government is that it plans to lend the farmers an additional $100 million. They seem to think that these loans are the only way they can help the farmers.
The fruit and vegetable industry in this country has suffered greatly. I should like to place on record some information that has been made available by the federation of agriculture. They point out that in the nine months just past we have imported over $7,500,000 more of fruits and vegetables than we did in the year before. I urge the government to look carefully into this matter. They have received deputations and petitions from the fruit and vegetable growers throughout Canada urging them to look into the tariff situation, so that the vegetable producers will have their seasons when fruit and vegetables from outside Canada are not permitted to come in. I do not believe the department has even looked at this problem, because last year we imported into Canada for nine months alone fruits and vegetables to a value of $32,499,000. The vegetable growers in the riding I have the honour to represent, notably those in the Holland marsh area, have sent petition after petition urging the government, not for a high tariff wall to be erected around their product, but rather

for regulations so that these products will not be allowed in at certain times, and so that in one year $10 million worth more of them will not come than came in in a previous year.
In conclusion I urge that the government give some thought to its $5 billion defence program in the next two or three years, and that at the same time it give thought to what may be done to help maintain agriculture in a better position, whether in a time of war or of peace. Because it is not fair to let agriculture slip as it has been slipping.
Then, in the matter of income tax, let me point out that only about 3i per cent of the total farm population in Canada, comprising some 700,000 people, have gross revenues from products sold, before making deductions for exemptions, interest on depreciation and interest on investment, of over $10,000 of gross income, and only 14 per cent have gross incomes of over $5,000. I say the government should have a clear-cut policy as to how these taxes are to be collected. I am sure that, in most cases, if the farmer took anything out as payment for managerial duties he would have no income tax to pay at all. I am not sure that the government needs so many people receiving high salaries racing up and down the concession lines of this dominion, men who know very little about agriculture, but who are hunting out the farmers and who are arbitrarily telling those farmers how much they ought to pay, how much they are worth, how much the housewife has been spending on mink coats, champagne and caviar, and telling her that she must have spent so much.
No one who understands agriculture believes that is a sound procedure. There should be some simpler form; I do not believe a farmer should have to hire a lawyer or an accountant to decipher many of the questions asked. The fact is that he is making only a fraction of what he is assumed to be making.

speechtext: Breaking with the fashion so recently established by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I am not going to demand that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) resume his place in the house while I am speaking. I realize that anything which I might add to this debate would hardly deter him or other members of the official opposition from continuing to launch their verbal broadsides at the frail form of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Rather I am moved to say that the superintendent of public functions, the financial critic, has portrayed his role with all the majesty and imperial zeal of a noble Roman tribune.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are only a few Liberals present.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know who has just said that there are only a few of my own party listening. Am I to take it that the opposition benches are completely vacant, more so than they usually are? Normally the task of the financial critic is an arduous one, but this year it was made even more difficult by the fact that the Minister of Finance announced that the Canadian people, because of their hard work and their success in developing this nation, would receive something in the nature of a social dividend or bonus in the form of tax relief.
With production and national income at an all-time high, with new mineral resources being exploited and developed, with the national debt drastically reduced, a broader application of the Liberal principle of fair distribution was declared to be in order. Add to this the fact that Canada continues to maintain her fair share of overseas assistance commitments and to maintain an enormous although necessary defence program, and one can readily appreciate the bleak reserve and
2476	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Riley silence with which members of the loyal opposition greeted the 1953-54 budget.
I am going to risk being repetitious and refer, as did the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lesage), to an editorial which appeared in the New York Times of February 21. In that editorial the writer said that the pale green look on the faces of New Yorkers of the day before had been envy. As a spectator of the drama here on the 19th, I wondered at the time if perhaps the pale green look in New York was not a reflection, brought about by some of these new-fangled rediffusion processes, of the dark green look which appeared on some of the faces of those in the front benches opposite.
When the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) rose he clutched his toga tightly to his body, from which by the way had been torn and eradicated all the brand marks of big business, and he proceeded with funereal intonations to dispel this aura of brightness and hope and confidence, which the people of Canada have in the future of their nation, and to enshroud his listeners with a rather dismal cloak of gloom. The budget was a bad budget. Sombrely and relentlessly, on and on he went primly and dutifully pointing out that this government, this group of shall we say dubious Canadians who sit on this side of the house, were guilty of extravagance, waste and mismanagement. Then he went on with the inevitable albeit modest inference that he himself might make a pretty good finance minister. I do not think ever before in the history of this country has there been a more pathetic application for a post in the public service.
My reaction to the budget was somewhat different from that of the hon. member for Greenwood. I welcomed the tax relief coming as it did in its various forms. I find it increasingly difficult to pay income tax. I have always regarded the radio licence and the stamp tax as nuisances. For a while after the 19th I felt a little elated for myself and my fellow New Brunswickers because the Minister of Finance had seen fit to relieve us of some of the cigarette tax. However, a couple of days later the new Progressive Conservative government in New Brunswick decided in their budget that they were going to place more taxes on cigarettes. Some of us are beginning to wonder how long it will be before they find means of reviving a direct tax on radio listeners in that province or new stamp taxes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Apparently the legislators in New Brunswick are not in accord with the hon. member for Greenwood and his New Brunswick colleagues here in Ottawa. After they had claimed that the minister had not taken off enough of the cigarette tax, they hastened to raise the price again. I suggest that there should be a federal-provincial conference of the Tory party.

speechtext: The Liberal government put on a sales tax that was not put on by the federal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Conservative government was going to take off the sales tax, but they have not done it yet. If the hon. member for Royal, who is constantly interrupting me, will come up to my office after I finish my speech I will give him quotations from some of his New Brunswick colleagues during the last provincial campaign when they said that as soon as they were elected they would wipe out the sales tax. There is no doubt that is what he wants me to put on record, so there it is. If he wants names, I will give them to him. To me as a maritimer, representing as I do a seaboard section of the Atlantic provinces, the most significant news in the budget speech was that dealing with southern trade. I was very pleased to hear the Minister of Finance tell us that trade with the Latin American countries amounted to $272 million during the last year, or more than double what it was in 1949. This is confirmation of the bright picture painted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on his return from the 20,000 mile trip which he recently made to these countries. I predict that the story of the success of that trip is going to find a permanent place in the annals of this nation. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce has ever doubted the Canadian people's appreciation of the tremendous achievements he has accomplished on their behalf over the past years, I think he can safely assume now that these doubts can be dispelled.

But the ministers did not tell all of the story. It could have gone on for hours describing how Peru, Bolivia, Mexico, Brazil, Panama and many other countries are willing and anxious to do business with Canada, and how favourable is our trade position with them at the present time. During the first nine months of 1952 our exports to Peru were nearly four times what they had been for the similar period of 1951. Our exports to Mexico amounted to 30 per cent more than what they had been for the similar period in 1951. Exports to Brazil more than doubled. We should take every advantage of this trend because to us in the Atlantic provinces it is very good news. These are our natural markets. These are the markets of which we should be taking advantage. These are markets, I might suggest to my Tory friends opposite, into which we do not have to blast our way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I enjoy these interruptions because they give me an opportunity to refer to some of the figures I have in my notes. Hon. members know that generally speaking the economy of the Atlantic provinces is lagging. Because of our unfavourable geographical location in relation to the heavily populated sections of the country, we are out of step with the booming economy of the nation. My heart has been particularly heavy this winter over the plight of the dock workers and longshoremen of the port of Saint
The audget-Mr. Riley John. Residents of the cities of Saint John and Lancaster have been suffering for want of freight going through our ports to the various markets of the world. A lot more freight might have gone through the ports of Saint John and Halifax if some of our Canadian industries were more prone to route their export traffic through our ports rather than through United States ports.
I am very glad that elsewhere yesterday some startling figures went on record pointing out to the public of Canada, and more particularly to the people of the maritime provinces, what shocking discrimination has been practised in respect of our ports. I might also tell the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), or I would tell him if he were in his place in the house but in his absence I will point it out to some of the other leaders over there, that if they would get in touch with some of their big business friends in this part of the country they might be able to suggest to them that they should begin routing some of their export traffic in manufactured products through the ports of Saint John and Halifax in increasing volume.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you no business friends up here?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not got as big business friends as has the Tory party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh dear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These gentlemen on the other side of the house are always talking about government interference with business and commerce. If something is not done with respect to routing Canadian manufactured goods through United States ports, it might be a good thing if we had a little government interference in business-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A change of government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-because the yawning indifference of some Canadian industries, whose products find ready markets in the maritime provinces, to the ports of Saint John and Halifax, is matched only by the failure of the life insurance companies to reinvest in our provinces a fair proportion of the huge premium income which they so gladly take from us each year. We who live in the Atlantic provinces live there because we love that part of Canada. Living there, we want to see an opportunity for our children whom we also want to live there. But prospects of such opportunity grow dimmer as the years go by. Lack of home markets and high freight tariffs retard our industrial expansion. For the most part profits flow back to the central part of Canada because we cannot meet competition. Were it not for the social

The Budget-Mr. Riley security program of the present administration and preceding administrations over the last 17 years-my Tory friends might also say "hear, hear" to this-were it not for some of those things like unemployment insurance, old age pensions, mothers' allowances and other benefits, the flow would be all in one direction.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Bowing to experience, I shall be very glad to take back what I said even though I did write it down at the time.
Speaking of old speeches by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), as a member from the Atlantic provinces, having regard to the fact that through this social security measure we get back some share of the profits which we send to other parts of Canada, I for one am not going to let the mothers of the Atlantic provinces forget that the Leader of the Opposition said that the family allowances bill was wicked and unjust.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Talk that one off.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How long ago was that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member asks how long ago that was. Well, it was not when the Leader of the Opposition was' a mere stripling of a boy. That was when the Leader of the Opposition was a mature-minded premier of the province of Ontario, a man who should be fully conscious of the enormity of the consequences of his words. Now, he may say that he did not say that the family allowances bill was wicked and unjust, but he did. He said it was iniquitous, and there are only two definitions for "iniquitous" in the Concise Oxford Dictionary. Those two definitions are "wicked" and "unjust". Therefore, I think that it is fitting that I, and every other Liberal member or every other man who might be a candidate in the forthcoming election, should remind the mothers of the Atlantic provinces that the Leader of the Opposition referred to the family allowances bill as being wicked and unjust.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it still his policy?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot say that it is still his policy. He has made statements since that appear to be somewhat contrary, but I have never heard him get up in the house and say: I did say that and I apologize to the mothers of Canada. I said that at a time when I was not a national leader but when I was representing a section of the country- and I take back everything that I said.
Getting back to southern trade, I have always felt that the ports of Saint John and Halifax could be kept busy or could be helped to be kept busy the year round by a constant flow of imports and exports to and from those markets. I have always felt that the industries of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland could be enormously stimulated by such trade. In the centre of those provinces lies Prince Edward Island, whose agricultural products could feed twice the population of the surrounding provinces with lots left over for export. With such a stimulus to industrial expansion, perhaps we might have an increased population in the maritime provinces. With increased population perhaps we might get home markets and then perhaps we could wave our hands at the high freight rates which we are now facing. With this in mind I am going to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to send another trade mission to the Latin American countries-a trade mission made up of representatives and businessmen from the Atlantic provinces.

It is no idle fantasy to suggest that the success of such a move by the Minister of Trade and Commerce might help to mark the beginning of a new era in our part of Canada. For, with the prospect of industrial expansion, we might find ourselves where we could easily have a more stable economy in the early future.
The story of the mineral deposits in northern New Brunswick is heartening news and, coming with that, news from New York that large financial interests have decided to carry on further exploration and development work in the New Brunswick oil fields brings a new ray of hope to the people in my part of Canada. The discovery of large deposits of refractory materials in and about the constituency of my hon. friend from Royal is also very encouraging.
I am going to suggest to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) that his department might inject a little more assistance into the development of the mineral potential of my province. I am going to suggest that perhaps he might put more geological survey crews in the field. I am going to ask him, in ithe light of the fact that our economy is lagging, and in the light of the fact that we need some extra stimulation, if his department will not be ready to come down to New Brunswick and make more diamond drilling equipment available-and perhaps give more impetus to the already encouraging prospect of large mineral finds within the boundaries of New Brunswick.
I might offer a suggestion to the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) as well. I could suggest to him that, now Canada is rapidly expanding and rapidly developing into one of the great nations of the earth, there is need for more imagination and more vision among the engineers of the various government departments, including his own. I might suggest to him that when the Boulder canyon project was first mooted it received rather cold treatment in the minds of most engineers; yet men of vision, men of foresight and men who had great confidence
The Budget-Mr. Riley in the future of their country pressed vigorously for the project, as they also pressed for the construction of the Tennessee valley projects. The fruits of these vast projects went beyond even their wildest dreams.
There may be great possibilities in the maritimes, great possibilities which are meritorious of more consideration by government engineers. I am thinking of projects like Passamaquoddy. I am not one of those who suggest that the Passamaquoddy power project should be constructed immediately. I am not even going to suggest that it is economically feasible. But I am going to suggest, as I have suggested to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that for the sum of $900,000 we in Canada can pay out share of the cost of a complete survey and find out once and for all whether or not the Passamaquoddy project is economically feasible. Having regard to the wealth of this country and having regard to the enormous boom which the larger sections of the country are experiencing, I do not think that is too much for the maritimes to ask for.
We are grateful for public works; we are grateful for anything. We are grateful for the social security program of the government. But we feel that at this time some greater impetus should be given to the development of those sections of the country which do not appear to have such vast mineral resources to be tapped as do others; which do not have such densely populated areas and which do not have such a rich industrial potential but which are none the less part and parcel of the country and should therefore be part and parcel of the national concern.
When I was speaking a few minutes ago about the potential of southern markets I neglected to mention the news; and I attribute this fact to the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), he having found it necessary to interrupt me so often.

I could hardly make up something the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said. When he was speaking here, as reported at page 1841 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
Our balance of trade with Cuba Is very much in our favour, and Cuba is a very important market to the maritime provinces. It always has been and it always will be. The Cuban agreement on raw sugar was made as a means of stimulating that market and of protecting the market we have had. It has had that effect. There has been a very sharp growth in imports from the maritime provinces, and in talking to the people of Cuba I may say that they in Cuba believe that market can be stimulated a great deal more.
It was necessary to conduct these negotiations with that thought in mind. Certainly I have no intention at any cost of disturbing that market for products of the maritime provinces.
He made that statement in answer to the Progressive Conservatives who in this house made an attempt to disrupt that market. I am sure that had the hon. members in the opposition known what I was going to quote, they might not have been so ready to listen to me.
To sum it all up, when the history is written of this proud epoch in the development of a great nation, I should hate to have my children read and be taught, perhaps in another part of this or another land, that the Atlantic provinces had lagged in the wake of Canadian progress like the back field of an abundantly productive farm; or I should hate to have my part of the country depicted as the dying limb of an otherwise luxuriantly foliaged tree, one of the main branches withering for want of proper circulation of the sap of national concern.

Mr. Speaker, I trust you will not believe that there is a barnyard to my extreme right. These clackings and quackings
The Budget-Mr. Herridge and mooings and brayings that you hear are coming from the member for Mackenzie.
I must get on with the few remarks that I wish to make in connection with this important subject. I am particularly, shall I say, embarrassed and pleased with the rather representative and attentive audience that I have here this afternoon. I am not going to deal in detail with the budget. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) did that very effectively the other day, and presented the views of this group so far as the budget is concerned. However,
I do wish to deal with a few aspects of the budget before proceeding with my pleas in connection with the need of the great host of unrecognized persons in Canada so far as this budget is concerned.
Before dealing with those things I wish to say in criticism of the budget I must say in fairness that some things are included in this budget that will be welcomed by the average Canadian citizen regardless of the party to which he belongs. I am sure the reduction in excise duty on cigarettes is welcomed by a large number of people. I know that since the reduction the manufacturers have dropped the price a cent or two a package. But I want to bring to the attention of the house the continuing discrimination against a certain group in this country in these budgets that are presented from year to year. We have legislation before the house to overcome discrimination as to race, creed and colour, and further proposals as to sex, and I am all in favour of these proposals. The Minister of Finance year after year continues to discriminate against the ancient order of dependable pipe smokers. I should like to know the reason for the failure to grant concessions to those who smoke cigars and pipes-
