I am pleased to have the cooperation of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. That will be the one little duty he has performed this session.
Everyone will be pleased with the exemptions allowed far dependent children attending university and over 21 years of age, with the raising of the permissible income for dependents from $600 to $750 and the allowance exemption for expenses on account of those elected to municipal office. That is a very reasonable proposal. In a good many of our city councils the aldermen give a very great deal of their time for little remuneration, and this is a very fair and justifiable provision.
With respect to the repeal of the sales tax on books, I am glad to say how pleased we are that the repeated pleas of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) in that respect have been listened to by the Minister of Finance. I notice that there is also repeal of the sales tax on newsprint. I am informed that that will mean a considerable sum to the large newspapers of this country. It is strange that within a few days of the government giving that tax concession to newspapers the paper manufacturers increased their price a considerable amount per ton.
We are all very pleased with the elimination of the $2.50 radio licence fee. It was a difficult fee to collect, and was not paid by quite a large percentage of the people. It was also a costly fee to collect. It will be generally accepted across Canada as a good move. I am of the opinion that the provision to use the 15 per cent excise tax on radios and radio equipment to finance the cost of the operation of the C.B.C. is a sound and constructive move on the part of this government and will be generally accepted across the country.
It was a good move to remove the nuisance tax on money orders, cheques and other instruments. We thought that was something of an institution that was going to continue forever, and therefore it came as a surprise vhen it was removed. But in view of the


labour of printing stamps, and the nuisance of attaching them to cheques and other documents, having in mind always the total revenue received, I think it was a wise provision.
Then we were particularly pleased-not because of the amount but because of the fact-when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) finally did give some heed to the repeated pleas of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for a reduction of the floor on medical expenses for income tax purposes. While there is only a reduction of 1 per cent, at least it is a start in the right direction; and we are pleased to note that the C.C.F. group in the house has made this small dent in the minister's armour. While there has been this reduction of 1 per cent, members in this group will continue to press for the complete removal of the floor.
In several budgets, if I remember correctly, the Minister of Finance has expressed concern about the high level of taxation on corporation profits, and he has now emphasized this concern by reducing the standard rate of corporation tax from 50 per cent to 47 per cent.

From evidence that has been placed before the house, and is now being presented to the defence expenditure committee, I am sure that same state of affairs applies in this country, and that with the elimination of waste and extravagance we could surely reduce our expenditures on defence to the extent of 10 per cent, and still have an effective defence effort.
The $120 million to which I have referred, plus a possible saving of $200 million in defence expenditures, provides us with $320 million. Had the government not reduced the corporation tax to the extent of $120 million, and if the government were to groom defence expenditures and go after those who are wasting money and acting extravagantly with government funds, we would have $320 million, and this without any change in the taxation of the country. I have only a moment to conclude this phase of my argument, and I trust hon. members opposite will consider it an argument. This group believe in income tax according to ability to pay. We believe that income tax, under this system of government, is the fairest way to secure funds for a better redistribution of wealth. I have mentioned that, as we think, the minister has reduced corporation taxes unnecessarily. Capital development is going on at a terrific pace in Canada. subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I adjourned the debate on the last occasion this bill was before the house, and at this time I have only one or two further points to make.
I said before that, if it could be worked out equitably, I did not have any great objection to the payment of farm storage. I said I felt that while I would be benefited personally by the passage of a bill of this kind, I felt there were certain inequalities in it, and I was inclined to agree with the chairman of the wheat board when he said that it should be looked at again.
Speaking generally, among farmers in western Canada the facilities for marketing wheat can well take care of the wheat offered from time to time. Of course we do have situations develop as we saw in 1952, when it becomes necessary to store certain amounts of wheat on the farms because facilities to take the wheat to market are not adequate. If in our normal experience we could expect this condition every crop year, and it became necessary to have large quantities of grain stay on the farms because of the inadequacy of facilities to handle it, there would be a certain necessity for this kind of legislation. However, in the normal year with the facilities available being sufficient to bring the grain to market, as I stated the last time I spoke, I feel that certain difficulties would be met in having the grain flow into position as rapidly as it should, and it might be necessary for the wheat board to requisition grain.
When the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) spoke he said that out of 112,000 farmers in Saskatchewan less than 8 per cent farm over 5 quarter sections, which is 800

Canadian Wheat Board Act acres, and fewer than 10 per cent were paying income tax. That would not be a very large percentage when we are dealing with over-all production. There is only one thing that bothers me. I could spend the next ten minutes naming farmers I know who farm anywhere from 3 to 15 sections. These men are always faced with the inadequacy of the quota. They can deliver enough under the initial quota to pay their expenses because the size of their operation gives them a greater efficiency. But under the quota system they are of necessity forced to retain a sizeable amount of grain on the farm.
That argument is backed up to a certain extent by table 8 of the taxation statistics for 1952, which shows that out of 112,000 farmers in Saskatchewan, 10,950 were taxpayers. Their taxable income was $40,596,000 and they paid $3,467,000 in taxes. That number of 10,950 approximates 10 per cent of the total number of farmers. The net income of the farm population of Saskatchewan in 1952 was $265,200,000, of which $40,596,000 was taxable, which gives you a figure between 15 and 20 per cent as representing the percentage of the net total farm income being received by from 8 to 10 per cent of the farmers.
These relatively few farmers who have this large net income are, as I said before, forced to keep a good deal of grain on the farm. Many of them have reasons other than their inability to deliver. They may desire to keep it on the farm for tax reasons, or they may want to have a certain carryover of wheat. I feel that if a system of farm storage payments was inaugurated it would not be a year to year business. As X have said, we do not need it most years although this year possibly we do.
If a system of farm storage payments was inaugurated there would be a good deal of pressure to continue it. A large number of the larger farmers would be helped. They are holding back anyway, and they would benefit every month by the increase in the initial price being made to take care of this farm storage. There are certain farmers who would be pleased to have this system, but I still have to be convinced that the greater number of farmers, that is the 103,000 odd excluding the 8 per cent, would be particularly anxious to have to sell their grain in the fall in order to pay their bills and then see a neighbour with a large farm benefiting from a rise in the price of wheat at the rate of a cent or half a cent a bushel per month to allow for storage charges.
There is nothing more that I wish to say on this particular matter. We have an


adequate marketing system through the Canadian wheat board. The chairman of that board has expressed an opinion-I do not know whether he did it publicly, but I believe he did it privately-that while there is a good deal of merit in the payment for farm storage, a further survey should be made of the matter. As I have said before, I am not particularly opposed to this, nor am I advocating it. The chairman of the wheat board has done a good job in handling the grain crop, and if he feels that the matter should be taken under consideration I think we should take a further look at it. He feels that the necessity for this measure is not pressing, and I believe we should consider it further.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer one or two of the questions raised by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson). He states that he does not think the small farmer would be benefited by this legislation, and that the large farmer would receive the greatest amount of benefit. If that is the case I cannot understand why the farm unions in western Canada, which I am sure represent the small farmer even more than they do the large farmer, are asking for this legislation.
The hon. member stated also that when grain was needed it might be necessary for the wheat board to requisition. If the wheat board needed grain at any time they could stop paying these storage charges. The bill does not make it compulsory for the wheat board to continue to pay storage charges for grain during the full season.
Another argument used by the hon. member is that the large farmers hold back grain for income tax purposes. That may have been true before the Income Tax Act was changed, but now the farmer can average his income over a five-year period and there would be no advantage in holding back grain. I do not think that argument is sound.
The main argument for this legislation, as I see it, is that under the conditions which exist in western Canada at the present time, and have existed for a number of years, the farmers in certain sections are able to deliver large quantities of grain early in the season. The way we are situated in western Canada we must get as much grain as possible to Port Arthur and Fort William before the season closes in early December. In order to get the greatest use of box cars, grain is hauled mainly from Manitoba and over the main line of the Canadian Pacific in the eastern part of Saskatchewan. Therefore you find that the quotas in these areas are raised to 15 bushels to the acre months before quotas

are raised in other parts of the western provinces. The result is that they get their grain out while farmers in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan, particularly, find that their quotas are not raised and they have to hold their grain on the farm whether or not they want to do so. 1 think we should have some compensation for that.
It is also true in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan, where at least some of our grain goes through the port of Churchill, that grain is held in storage in the elevators so that it can be moved to Churchill in the latter part of July and the first part of August before the new grain comes on the market. That results in a large amount of grain in that area having to be held on the farms, and we think we should have some advantage from the storage of that grain. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) introduced a resolution asking for payment for grain properly stored on the farms, and I think this bill would help to solve some of the difficulties and iron out some of the inequities that exist in the marketing of our grain in western Canada. It would give the farmers some incentive to build storage on the farms, and I know of no better insurance that any farmer can have than a granary full of properly stored grain on his farm.
I think we should try to have anything that would encourage that put into legislative form. I know that in the 1930's and in the years when we have had drought in western Canada-and drought will recur-nothing gave more security to the farmer than a granary or two of grain stored on his own farm. If this legislation were put into effect it would encourage farmers to provide their own insurance against years of drought.
As long as we have these large carryovers of grain, and we are likely to have them for the next two or three years at least, I think this bill would provide a fair division of the amount of storage which we are having to pay. At the present time the elevator companies are building additional storage space. They are only doing so because they know that space is going to be paid for through the grain that will be stored in it over the next few years. I think we should encourage our farmers to build storage space on their own farms and store grain there so that it will be in position.
I remember that a few years ago in the area which I represent grain had to be shipped back from Winnipeg and the head of the lakes for seed purposes. Because of a short crop the grain had all gone out in the fall of the year before. There was no encouragement to hold it, and the result was that grain shipped in the fall and paid for at the
Canadian Wheat Board Act rate of 80 cents a bushel was bought back by the farmers in the spring at $1.25 a bushel for seed purposes, and freight was paid on it from that area to Fort William and back again. I think this is proper legislation, and something which would benefit the farmers of western Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it was last session that I spoke about grain handling and grain storage in northwestern Saskatchewan. I do not intend to take a great deal of the time of the house on this topic on this occasion, but I should like to say a few words about a government interior storage elevator that we should like to see erected at North Battleford. In this connection I might say that I have the endorsations of some 13 rural municipalities surrounding the city of North Battleford and also endorsations of certain farm union lodges.
So far as grain storage is concerned, there is something I should like to draw to the attention of the house. We read in the press ait the present time that considerable insect damage is being done to farm-stored grain. In the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of February 16, 1953, there is the following Canadian Press dispatch from Regina:
R. E. McKenzie, director of the agriculture department's plant industry branch, said here that a large number of insects apart from the rusty grain beetle are damaging farm-stored grain in Saskatchewan. He said the common grain mite and the rusty grain beetle are the principal insects which damage the kernel of the grain, but investigation had also revealed the presence of other insects which merely live in the grain but can cause heating and spoiling. He urged farmers to examine their bins and piles carefully, taking samples from top to bottom.
There is also another article in the Manitoba Co-operator of December 18, 1952, which reads as follows:
Infestations of farm-stored grain by the rusty grain beetle have occurred in Alberta and Saskatchewan. This insect feeds on grain in storage and when present in large numbers causes the grain to heat and go out of condition. The result is loss in germination and deterioration in baking quality, according to F. L,. Watters, officer in charge, dominion Department of Agriculture laboratory of entomology, Winnipeg.
With respect to grain storage, I am of the opinion in so far as northwestern Saskatchewan is concerned that a greater number of farmers might benefit from the erection of a storage elevator at North Battleford. I think we will all agree that quotas are here to stay. In the Livestock Times of Saskatoon for February 6, 1953, there is the following:
The change from horses to mechanical power on farms has released 70 million acres for food production in the United States in the past forty years.
2486	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act
I do not know the figures tor Canada but I would say that the same proportion would apply here. Therefore I am of the opinion that, with the coming of farm tractors and with land still being broken up, regardless of any change in the system of marketing grain in western Canada we are still going to have the quota system.
Speaking of quotas, there is one thing I should like to suggest for the smaller operator, and I believe we should be considering the smaller operator in western Canada. I refer to the farmer's son who starts out on a half section or three-quarter section of land, and to our returned soldiers. To assist them in financing, I think there should be a minimum quota, and I would say 750 bushels. I was going to say 1,000 bushels but that might interfere a little too much with the first quota that might be delivered by all farmers, large and small. For the purpose of assisting the small operator and the returned soldier who starts out on a rather small farm, and who may not own combining and threshing machinery, I think consideration should be given to the establishment of a minimum quota.
In at least three periods when grain crops in the northwestern part of Saskatchewan have been good, in the twenties, the early forties and the last two years, the question of inadequate grain handling facilities in that part of the province has been a very serious one and the situation has been detrimental to the growers. With a view to alleviating the situation, recommendations have been made to Ottawa for the building of an interior storage elevator with cleaning and drying facilities. In connection with the erection of such an elevator, I might add that we saw in the thirties, and it might happen again, that these elevators could be used to a great extent for the storage of grain to meet seed grain requirements.
I think that is something that should be considered when we are talking about storing grain. Opinions differ as to what is the best thing to do to meet the situation. Some people advocate building more terminal facilities at the eastern seaboard. Others urge increased elevator facilities at Churchill, and some advocate requesting the authorities to pay storage to farmers rather than to construct interior elevators.
As we understand the situation, the greatest need for increased facilities today is during the harvest season when so many thousands of farmers are combining or threshing, and at the same time hauling grain to elevators or granaries as long as there is room. It appears to me that additional elevator facilities at an eastern seaport would be of no assistance to farmers in


northwestern Saskatchewan, when the accommodation is most needed. Additional facilities at Churchill would be an advantage to the prairie provinces as a whole and are undoubtedly desirable, but here again the added facilities would not meet the requirements of farmers in northwestern Saskatchewan when most needed.
There is no question at all but that in years when the crop is average or better than average, there would be a lot of grain left on the farms even after a four or five million bushel elevator had been filled and hundreds of carloads had been dispatched for export. It seems to me that nearby storage is what is most required.
This northwestern area, which is close to 20 per cent of the grain-growing portion of the province, is the largest area in the prairie provinces not at present served by an interior storage elevator. Elevators at Calgary and Edmonton serve the grain-growing portion of Alberta; elevators at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw provide facilities for central and southern parts of Saskatchewan. In southeastern Saskatchewan and Manitoba the crop is usually ten days to two weeks earlier than up here, and much of it is shipped to Winnipeg or elsewhere before car shortage becomes a problem.
If an interior storage elevator is built in northwestern Saskatchewan, we presume there is no argument but that it should be in North Battleford, where practically all the highways and railways of the area converge. There is an additional reason for having an interior storage elevator at a central point near the area of production. The grain could be shipped to eastern or western points, or to Churchill, or to interior points for home consumption, without any back-haul expense.
In so far as the resolution before us is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I think the greater number in my area would be getting more benefit if such an elevator were constructed in North Battleford because what the farmer wants to do, especially the average farmer, is to get out 10 or 15 bushels per acre as soon as possible in order to pay his running expenses. I think he requires that more than farm storage.
An elevator there in my particular area would be the best thing that could be done in connection with farm storage, taking into account the system of quota delivery as we have it today. As I have said previously, I think quotas are here to stay. No matter what system we have for marketing grain there is bound to be a system of quotas in order to give everyone a fair shake when it comes to delivering to the elevator.

I do believe that the minimum quota for the small operator should have consideration by the department. As I have said, our small operators and our soldiers who are starting up on a half section or three-quarter section will have an opportunity to pay their harvest expenses. Many of them do not own threshing and combining machines, but they would have an opportunity of meeting their running expenses and paying the owners of the machines who come in and harvest their crops.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I will just take a couple of minutes. I want to support this legislation introduced by the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and supported by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I can save time by not repeating what they said but I think pretty much as they do.
I think that this legislation should be popular because it will not cost the taxpayer any money. I know that on the branch lines where the quota was small, owing to the scarcity of box cars at different points, it would have been a big benefit last year.
I know that merchants along some of the branch lines were laying out $15,000 or $20,000 in credit. The farmer was willing to pay, but he had only so many bushels of grain. If he had been paid for his storage he could have made a token payment on his bill with the storekeeper.
I was talking about this legislation outside of the house and someone I was talking with said that the big farmers would hold their grain indefinitely. Well, that is taken care of in the bill. There is provision that the wheat board may see that that does not take place. The wheat board can say that the storage is off and that they need the grain. That would take care of it so I do not think we need worry about a farmer holding grain.
My hon. friend from The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) has mentioned damage to grain by mites, and that sort of thing. We have always had them, and I had them on my own farm. If we wake up to what the people in the grain division tell us we can take care of it the same as they do in the big elevators.
I have much pleasure in supporting the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke at
some length on this bill when it was before the house last session, and I do not propose to repeat what I said then.
The proposal is that the wheat board, out of funds belonging to all producers, will pay
Canadian Wheat Board Act storage on the farm for those who do not or cannot deliver their grain immediately after the harvest. I think it is fair to point out that if every producer had the same yield per acre and if the quota system were working uniformly across Canada, the payment of farm storage would leave every producer just where he would have been anyway, as far as final returns are concerned, except that there would be the additional mechanics of working out the storage adjustment.
I might point out to the last speaker that it would not be income to the farmer until he delivered his grain, because farm storage would only be paid, of course, when the grain is delivered. In other words it is of very little value to the farmers, assuming that the crops are about uniform and assuming that quotas are reasonably uniform across Canada.
At the present time-within a few days- we expect to have a uniform 15 bushel per acre quota right across the prairie provinces. Therefore no one would benefit from the payment of storage at the present time. However, assuming that crops are widely different as they are in some years, it would mean that the man with the small crop would bonus the man with the big crop. There is no doubt about that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
The man with the small crop
would be forced to deliver his crop because he would need the money immediately. The man with the big crop could deliver sufficient to pay his running expenses, hold the rest and collect storage on it.
Another feature of it is that it is a case where the poor bonus the rich. The poor man, however large his crop, needs to deliver it immediately to meet his immediate commitments. The rich man can say: "Well, it is paying a very nice return to me where it is; it is better than a bond. I will keep it, collect all the storage I can and deliver it in the spring." Then it has the effect of crippling the board in its endeavour to get the best possible return for the farmers' grain. As I pointed out last year, the winter market for coarse grain is the best market; and grain marketed in the winter months will bring to the board a better return than will wheat marketed in June and July. I demonstrated that fact by figures. I checked up the figures this year and they indicate exactly the same result.
The suggestion has been made that it is exactly the same thing to have grain in store in a country elevator as to have grain in store on the farm. From a practical marketing viewpoint there is all the difference in
2488	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act The world. The grain in the country elevator is in the possession of the wheat board. The wheat board owns the grain in the elevator. They can sell it. They can do what they like with it. It is their grain. They have made an advance payment on it. On the other hand, grain on the farm is not in the possession of the wheat board and it cannot be sold until it is delivered to the board. The board cannot go short. They cannot sell what they do not have. There is therefore no analogy at all between storage in a country elevator where the grain is owned by the wheat board and storage on the farm where the grain is owned by the producer and where delivery of the grain depends entirely upon the whim of the producer.
I know of no organization, except the farmers' union, which favours this proposal.
I have talked with the leaders of the three pools. They see nothing in it whatever for the producer. In addition to that, I have talked to individual farmers and they see no benefit from it. I think it is distinctly a minority of prairie opinion which is in favour of this measure. I know that the wheat board have explored the matter thoroughly, and I know that the wheat board believe that it would be of no benefit to the producer. Mr. Mclvor so expressed himself at a meeting of the farmers' union at Edmonton, and also at two or three other annual conventions of prairie producers.
I do not know that I need to say more, Mr. Speaker. I know a great deal against the bill and I know nothing for it. I have heard in favour of this bill no good argument that will really stand up to analysis. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as the minister responsible for the administration of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, I cannot vote in favour of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with regard to this bill. It seems to me that this debate has taken a strange trend in that we have had the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) supporting this bill. The funny thing about it is that the people he represents are the people who are forced to sell their grain first. Manitoba has always been about a week, ten days or two weeks ahead of the people in the northwestern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The northeastern corner of my constituency comes alongside Manitoba. That is one reason I am definitely against this bill. The simple fact is that my farmers would have to sell.
There is a clause which provides that if the board called for the grain to be delivered,


it would have to be delivered; and if it was not delivered, this storage would stop. In the second place, the grain that has been threshed in western Canada for these last two years has naturally caused a kind of agitation for this measure, but it has been on account of the big crop and the two crops together. But I am sure if it was stated definitely to the farmers that one farmer pays the other farmer, there would be no support for this bill. I cannot understand why the C.C.F. party, which feels so strongly about co-operation, expect the little farmer to pay for the big farmer. You cannot get away from the fact that it is going to have that effect, that the little man is going to pay for the big man. There is no other way out of it.
The simple reason is that this man is obliged to sell. If I have 10,000 bushels of grain and they are going to give me 4 per cent, 5 per cent or 6 per cent on my money, I am going to hold the grain. If the wheat board says that I must sell it then it will be an unfair proposition because some other fellow somewhere else is going to try to hold his grain. If you get into an intricate system of forcing people to deliver grain at certain times, it is going to be so intricate that it will simply be impossible to handle.
As to the farmers' union, I am satisfied that this resolution would never have been passed in a convention of that kind if it had been properly explained to the people on the floor of the convention that one farmer was going to pay the other farmer. Many of these farmers think the wheat board is paying the elevator companies and that as they are paying the elevator companies, they might just as well pay the farmers.
Let us consider how many millions of bushels just go into the elevator, into the box car and away they go. If we are talking about grain that is being stored while the elevator is being filled until it is full to the top, surely you do not want that stuff out on the farm. You want it there. You want it so that you can get it in position to be sold. Our main business in western Canada is not storing grain; it is growing it and selling it. We must get it in position to sell it. We do not want to say to the farmer in Manitoba or to the farmer in western Alberta:	You have to sell your
grain; you have to get rid of it. We do not want the wheat board to say that. What we want to do is stick to our quota system and try to get the grain out as fast as we can possibly get it out; and when you get that grain out and get it in selling position, as the minister has just told us, you can

get a good price for it and you can put it in a position where the rest of the world can come and get it.
There is another thing I should like to say and it is this. Once you set up a system of this kind, by saying that you have to deliver this grain you are going to have more kicks than you will have under the system you have now. If you have an ordinary normal crop, as I said before, it is our business to get rid of it; that is when the quotas are up to around 15 bushels in an ordinary year, and when the average of wheat in western Canada runs about 17 or 18 bushels to the acre. Of course, these last two years the average has run from 23 to 24 bushels to the acre. That makes a great deal of wheat and a great deal of handling. Naturally the elevators get full and the fellow out on the farm figures that he should get just as much for storing the grain as does the elevator company. I agree with him. But it is maybe in only one or two years in ten that this would happen.
I say right now that the best thing to do is leave this with the wheat board. They are handling it and doing a wonderful job. The farmers are very well satisfied with it. They are satisfied to carry this thing along the best way they can. As the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) just said, you cannot take care of the grain out in the country. You get mites in it, and when you get mites in it there is only one thing to do with it, and that is turn it. They can turn it in the elevator and fix it up so that they do not lose too much of the grain. If it is on the farm, the farmer has to turn it. How is he going to do that? He has to have another bin some place or take a few loads to the elevator so he can turn it. In the old days it was easy to ask the elevator man to take a few loads, and it would be possible for him to keep on turning his grain so that the mites would die. Now he is under the quota system and it is not possible to do that. Therefore he gets into trouble in storing the grain.
The main and burning question in my mind is this. Let us stay with the wheat board and let them settle the situation that exists in western Canada. They will get rid of the grain as they have always done and we shall have a fair price. We will not have much of a carryover, and if we get up to a quota of 20 bushels to the acre at the start of the next crop year I think you will say that we have had a good job done by the wheat board, and we should thank them for it.

I say that the vast majority of producers would support and do support legislation such as this.
I noticed in the speeches made by members in the Liberal party that two of them, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) and the minister were strongly opposed to the measure. I noticed that the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) shifted from one foot to the other. He said he did not see much value in it and he did not see much disadvantage in the legislation. The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) really spoke about something else. That suggests to me that we do need farm storage.
The hon. member for The Battlefords said that there should be an interior elevator in his area. He makes that demand now mainly because there is no farm storage paid. If there were farm storage of some type that demand would not exist to the same extent in that area. I certainly would not oppose an interior elevator in his area if such were to be built. But I say the very fact that you have the hon. member asking for the expenditure of a large amount of money to build an interior elevator shows that there is a real problem that needs to be dealt with, and legislation such as this would be of great value to the western farmer.
The main argument of the minister is that this bill is merely for the rich farmer; that the poor will be contributing to the rich. That is a rather strange statement after the budget this government has brought down. Suddenly the members of the government take a great interest in the poor farmer who they say will have to pay storage to the rich farmer. Right today the farmers as a group are paying storage to the elevator companies, and the elevator companies are increasing their storage capacity. Therefore you are making the farmers as a group pay storage to the elevator companies, and the elevator companies are getting the cream in storage payments. As long as we have large quantities of grain that cannot be marketed we are going to have those elevator facilities continually expanded, and each year more and more money will be paid to the

As a farmer I would rather

It has been mentioned in this debate that mites get in the grain and so on and so forth. Perhaps the farmers in my area know how to store grain better than they do in other areas, but I doubt that. However, I do not know of a single farmer who has ever .lost a granary full of grain on his farm. I know farmers who have had their grain damaged; I do not know one who has lost a single bin of grain. Therefore this talk about mites and the danger of grain spoiling does not mean anything to me.
The hon. member for Mackenzie said, using himself as an example, "If I produced 10,000 bushels of wheat, then I would keep it all at home and I would get storage." Well, he might. There might be a few farmers who would do that, but they would be an insignificant percentage. I would rather see the hon. member for Mackenzie, if he were producing 10,000 bushels of wheat and wanted to keep it at home in order to get storage, keep it at home as a farmer and get that storage so that some of the little fellows would have a better opportunity early in the fall to deliver their grain. If the 10 per cent of farmers who pay income tax are going to keep a slightly higher quantity of grain at home, then certainly the smaller farmer will benefit by being able to haul his grain to the elevator at an earlier time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just before the debate was adjourned at five o'clock I had commended the minister for certain proposals in the budget which appear very fair to this group. I had commended him for listening to a succession of appeals with respect to certain matters that have been made by this group in recent years. I had criticized him for giving relief to the corporations of Canada to the extent of $120 million in one year as provided in the budget. I had suggested that if he had retained this $120 million and had saved $200 million by eliminating waste and extravagance in the defence department in the same proportion as suggested by the United States commission, which reported for that country that if waste and extravagance were eliminated in the United States defence program a reduction of 10 per cent in expenditure could be made with no loss of efficiency or security, the minister would then have had a total of $320 million with which to do something for the large number of forgotten people in this budget.
I should like to make this point before proceeding to indicate to the house the groups that have made pleas to the government and the house throughout the years. We are possibly experiencing the most prosperous period Canada has ever enjoyed. That was indicated by the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) yesterday afternoon, and it is very clearly indicated in the white paper issued under the minister's authority which I received in the mail this morning. Its title is "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1953". The opening sentences of the white paper are as follows:
The capital expenditure intentions of business, institutions and governments and of individuals for housing for 1953 involve an outlay of $5-4 billion. If this program is realized it will mean that capital expenditures in 1953 will be 6 per cent greater in value terms than the previous record of $5-1 billion accomplished in 1952.
My point is that we are experiencing continued and unusual prosperity, and if we are going to do anything for the people who have requested assistance from the government and parliament, when can we better do it than under present conditions? With the $320 million to which I have referred, which the government would have if it would take the action I have suggested, we could very well remove the means test from pensions for the blind. Such action is supported by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and by many other groups and organizations.
Only two days ago I received a letter from a constituent of mine who has been blind


since birth. He receives the blind pension of $40 a month. He has a small garden, grows a little fruit, keeps a few chickens, goes out in the woods and cuts and saws his own wood and cares for himself. He is an independent, very small subsistence farmer. He writes to me and says: "Why at my age in life should I be subjected periodically to investigation as to my financial resources and so on, when it is obvious to anyone that all I have is the $40 a month and the very small amount I can contribute toward my upkeep from my activities on my own acre or so"? Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we could very well remove the means test from pensions for the blind.
I think we could have increased the monthly payments for old age security. The government could also have given consideration to the proposals of the Canadian Legion. No one in this house will say that the Canadian Legion makes irresponsible demands. No one will say that the Canadian Legion goes before the cabinet and asks for something that is not sound and is not necessary and is not urgently needed.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I just want to refer briefly to the presentation to the cabinet by the dominion officials of the Canadian Legion on November 12, 1952. Mr. Speaker, when the minister was drafting this budget, it would appear to me that he listened to the appeals of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and big business, rather than to the appeals of the groups that have been forgotten as far as this budget is concerned. This brief, Mr. Speaker, gives in some detail the situation which the Legion finds in the country with respect to needy veterans. It makes certain recommendations.
The Legion recommends that allowances similar to those paid on behalf of the children of pensioners be granted children of war veterans' allowance recipients. It recommends that where an allowance is granted on behalf of an incapacitated child over the age of 21, this be continued on the death of the surviving parent; that the federal government initiate a policy for the children of deceased servicemen similar to that in force for single student veterans attending university or vocational training schools and receiving a monthly allowance under the rehabilitation act. The Legion recommends that veterans of world war I who served only in the United Kingdom be granted war veterans allowance.
I want to refer to these veterans particularly. Some of these veterans have been in Canada 30 or 35 years and served with the

British commonwealth of nations forces, but because they were not residing in Canada at the time they served in the first great war they are still denied the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Surely if we can, give $120 million to the corporations of this country we can consider this small group of men in Canada whose case has to date been by-passed by this government.
The Legion recommends that widows whose husbands had service which qualified them for war veterans allowance be granted the allowance if they are prevented from accepting remunerative employment for any reasonable cause. They further recommend that widows of allied ex-servicemen be granted war veterans allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada, provided that the widow herself has 20 years' residence and her husband was otherwise eligible. I am sure every veteran member of this house will agree with that proposal.
The Legion also recommends that Canadian veterans resident outside Canada but otherwise qualified be granted war veterans allowance. That is to serve the needs of certain veterans who have to live in California or other climates because of disabilities which prevent them from living their lives out in this country.
The Legion recommends that any definition of casual earnings be generous and broad and that any earnings, whether regular or not, be categorized as casual if they are small enough to be considered inconsequential in the light of existing wage levels. They also recommend that section 4 be amended so that either the veteran or his wife might be free to take employment and still enjoy the benefits of this section.
In that connection I know of the case of a veteran of the first world war with three daughters who were quite clever. The only way it was possible for them to attend university was for the mother to go out working. This veteran received war veterans allowance, but he made a mistake and failed to notify the board that the wife was earning extra money. She earned something over $1,000 and used every cent of it to pay for the education of those children at the university. This was discovered and the man, under the present regulations, must pay back the sum by monthly deductions.
I will say, in fairness to the officials of the board, that they are most sympathetic and give every consideration to these cases, but naturally they are there to give effect to the law and to the regulations.
The Budget-Mr. Herridge
The Legion recommends that perquisites be not considered as income under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and that unless fraud is established no recovery be made under section 19 of that act. They recommend that the ceilings on permissible income be increased to $1,200 a year for single men and $2,000 for those who are married.
I wonder if the minister and the cabinet gave consideration to the representations of the Canadian Legion and the needs of thousands of veterans of this country when they made a present of $120 million to the corporations of Canada.
I have on my desk, Mr. Speaker, briefs from the Canadian non-pensioned veterans' widows association, from the Silver Cross Women of Canada and from the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society. I am not suggesting we can do all that is proposed in these briefs, but surely we can do something more for these people who are suffering want and are in need in this country at this time.
I wonder if the minister gave consideration to the provision of assistance to those people who are unable to work and earn a living. I think the majority of members in this house believe that something should be done for those disabled who are not covered by legislation, those v/ho are unable to earn a living. What consideration has been given to increasing family allowances? I just mention these things and give these facts as illustrations of the groups of people who have been entirely forgotten according to the terms of this budget.
I have to hurry along now, Mr. Speaker, as I see that my time is passing quickly, but I want to refer briefly to housing and to one other matter that concerns the residents of my constituency. I enjoyed the speech by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) yesterday. I think he made an excellent contribution to this debate when he spoke on housing.

I am not going to notice the impertinent interjection of my friend as I only have a few minutes left; but I wonder if the minister thought of possible benefits of subsidized low rental housing for some of these workers who move from place to place and are living under very unsatisfactory conditions at present.
I wonder if he thought of the fruit industry in British Columbia; and before concluding I just want to say a word or two in that connection. The policy of the British Columbia fruit growers' association is to discuss their problems with the Canadian horticultural council, with members of the British Columbia federation of agriculture, with members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and with the federal and provincial governments. I am sure the Minister of Finance is fully aware of the problem that has been created for certain fruit growers, particularly for growers of soft fruits, owing to the change in financial policy and as a result of exchange regulations and the exchange situation with respect to the Canadian and United States dollars.
I know the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), who is a cabinet minister from British Columbia, has full knowledge of this subject, and I know he is doing all he can to make representations on behalf of the fruit industry of British Columbia. I know that he is willing to render every assistance that he can and co-operate with that industry to find some solution for the problem that faces the soft fruit industry in particular at this time.
The total apple production last year was such in Canada and the United States that the growers received fairly reasonable terms. However, the soft fruit producers experienced a very poor year for two reasons:	first, the
very heavy crop in the United States and in British Columbia; and second, because of the change in relationship of the Canadian and United States dollars.
The first inclination of many people is, naturally, to suggest higher tariffs, but I belong to a party which believes in lowering tariffs if possible and in stimulating world trade. Therefore, in view of our general approach to the world trading situation, our obligations to the United Nations, and the general demand for increasing the flow of trade between countries, I do not think we can properly ask for higher tariffs to remedy this situation.


In view of the fact that the soft fruit growers' difficulties are to some extent caused by action taken by the Minister of Finance, I suggested this government has in their case a particular responsibility for measures to remove this injustice. I further suggest that on that account a floor price for soft fruits should be established this year and that the government, in co-operation with the industry, should make every effort to increase markets for tree fruits at home and abroad.
I had intended, Mr. Speaker, to speak at somewhat great length on this subject. I shall return to it in a later debate, but I thought I ishould mention it on this occasion. When the Minister of Finance gave $120 million to the corporations of Canada, I wonder whether he thought of what should be done about a floor price for any section of the agricultural industry which needs stabilizing at this time, and for these people who need the assistance of a floor price.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, our point of view in this group is that while corporations and large industries in Canada reap the harvest provided by this government in this budget there are thousands who will continue to need help which, with fairer budgetary arrangements, we could so easily give.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who listened intently to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) deliver his budget address a week ago Thursday and heard the cheering, I came to the conclusion that there was more cheering than cheer in the budget.
I now want to refer to a couple of remarks made by the hon. member who has just spoken. One was with reference to the Agricultural Prices Support Act which, to all intents and purposes, has been thrown out the window, and the other was in reference to the brief we have received from the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. I wish to support their brief at this time.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) complained rather bitterly and at some length about the plight of the maritimes. My one comment on that complaint would be that they are suffering from 17 years of Liberal misrule.
Some praise was passed out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who has returned from a tour of the South American countries. Every Canadian hopes that trade will be extended in every direction. I was a bit perturbed to hear that some money was going to be spent on Mexican ports, because I believe there are many ports along the great lakes, in the maritimes and on the Pacific coast that could stand a bit of improving and fixing also. When I think of the Ming Sung

ships and the $12 million which we had invested in them and which slipped away, I feel that our foreign investments so far have not turned out to be paying propositions so far as dividends are concerned but have been a matter mostly of hopes. I think we had better look after some of our own ports before we start to be good fellows for all the people around the world. By the way, Mexico did not participate in either of the two world wars; therefore I think they should be able to look after their own ports.
I suggest that no government in history has lost more markets for primary products of this country than has this government. It does not take a great deal of ability-and I have said this before in the house-to sell scarce goods for less than they are worth; and that is what was done all through the war years. But it does take ability to sell surplus goods for more than they are worth; and that is something I have not seen this government doing yet.
Just yesterday, I believe it was, in the other place one of the senators from the maritimes was referring to the loss of shipping out of the Atlantic seaboard ports. After all, that means loss of trade and loss of business; and the labouring people who work on the docks are seeing their jobs being taken by labourers in another country. That is something the hon. member for Saint John-Albert also referred to.
Before I go on to some remarks about the budget, may I say that on February 23 I addressed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and I am going to read it. It is to be found at page 2293 of Hansard and reads as follows:
I wish to direct two questions to the Minister of Agriculture. Have instructions been issued to the government veterinarians not to take blood tests until March 2 of purebred cattle sold for delivery in the United States during the first week in March? Is the minister aware that such instructions will cause delay in delivery and financial loss to the livestock industry?
The next day the Minister of Agriculture replied. His reply may be found at page 2333 of Hansard. I am not going to quote the whole of his reply, but in part it reads as follows:
I have made inquiries and find that under date of February 20 instructions were issued to all district veterinarians that it was expected the embargo against the importation of cattle and livestock products into the United States from Canada would be removed on March 1 . . .
In other words, the instructions were just the apposite to that suggested by the hon. member, and the department had already taken action to see that there would be the minimum of delay in such movement so that there would be no financial loss to the livestock industry.
The Budget-Mr. H. O. White
Mr. Speaker, such is not the case. Here in my hand I have a telegram signed by one of the livestock producers in my county. He says:
Many March freshening cows have been sold for export March 1. Federal Department of Agriculture refuses to collect blood samples until lifting of embargo. This will cause much confusion among veterinarians and delay shipment some days-
This telegram was received at 3.32 p.m. on February 19. Within the next five minutes I called up the departmental officials and they got into quite an argument with me, saying that they were not going to take samples because they did not want to offend the Americans. I replied by saying that the Americans did not care whether or not they offended us when they shut off our dairy products, and they do not care whether or not they offend us when they bring in fresh fruit, fresh vegetables or what not. They do not wait for a week or two weeks. As soon as the day comes, they bring them in. I will name the gentleman to whom I spoke. It was Dr. Childs. He finally agreed to send out the instructions. On Tuesday, February 24, I received a telegram from the Middlesex Holstein association, signed by its president, and reading as follows:
Middlesex Holstein association request permission from government for T.B. kits to be released so Holstein cattle can be tested. Ready for shiD-ment to United States.
Then the next day I had a telegram from the same gentleman saying that the kits had been released on the 24th. This telegram was signed on the 25th, but the kits were released on the 24th. This morning I had a letter from the first gentleman who asked me to take action to see that testing was commenced immediately and not to wait until March 1. He says:
Would like to pass the following on to you About two weeks ago the Department of Agriculture, London, advised a neighbour that nothing would be done until the embargo was lifted On February 19 Dr. Harrison of Aylmer' was refused blood kits and forms. He was informed that instructions from the department were to the effect that no blood test would be taken until the embargo was lifted.
The minister turned right around and left the impression that my information to the house that day was not correct. Just because the minister wants to play politics, I will play the game myself.

It is difficult to conceive any plan or procedure which would do more to underwrite future employer-employee harmony and prosperity than the deferred proat-sharing plan which this enlightened American corporation has installed.
The brief sets out the philosophy of profitsharing in this way:
An employer installs a profit-sharing plan because he believes his shareholders will receive greater dividends as the result of the increased productivity of his employees and the increased stability of his labour force.
An employee accepts employment with and continues in the employment of an employer having a profit-sharing plan became he believes his productivity will be rewarded and because he enjoys the feeling of direct participation in the success or failure of an enterprise-a feeling otherwise enjoyed only by shareholders and management.
The basic goal of a profit-sharing plan is to create a common interest between the employees and the shareholders. Speaking in the broad and long-term sense, if this common interest cannot be created, we can only look forward to increasing industrial strife as the battle over the cutting up of the economic pie continues. We believe the inevitable long-term result of industrial strife is socialism as the only higher authority, government, is likely to be called upon with increasing frequency to intervene.
Such situations have already arisen.
If employees' remuneration is to be forever tied to uniform negotiated wage levels; if, unlike doctors, lawyers, farmers and other individual entrepreneurs, their remuneration cannot be directly related to their productivity; if they are not allowed to see the relationship between what they produce and what they earn; it is only natural that they will lose interest in a system which is supposed to be founded upon rewarding individual enterprise.
The brief then goes on to point out the difference between an immediate and deferred profit-sharing plan, and I quote:
There is nothing in present legislation to prevent an employer from installing an immediate profitsharing plan. Such a plan distributes cash on an annual or more frequent basis to employees in accordance with the employer's profits. The employer can write off such profit-sharing payments and the employees pay income tax on such payments just as though they were wages.
And again:
The concept of a deferred profit-sharing plan is quite different. The employee must be paid a good going wage, sufficient to maintain him on the standard of living considered reasonable in view of the type of work he is doing. Employer's profitsharing contributions, although allocated to the employee contingently, are made available only when they are really needed; when the employee dies, when he leaves after a certain number of years of service or when he retires.
And again:
Section 71A of the present Income Tax Act specifically requires an employee to pay income tax currently on employer contributions contingently allocated to his account in the trust fund. Since a deferred profit-sharing plan will almost always


incorporate a vesting schedule which withholds any right to the employer's accumulated profitsharing contributions until the employee leaves at retirement or terminates after completing a certain number of years of service, section 71A not only requires the employee to pay tax currently on income to which he has no immediate right, but also requires him to pay tax on income which he himself in many cases will never receive. Obviously it is difficult to set up a deferred profitsharing plan under such unfavourable legislation.
And finally:
After carefully examining all other possible solutions, we have come to the conclusion that the only' practical solution to the tax problem of deferred profit-sharing plans is to amend section 71A of the Income Tax Act in such a manner that:
(a)	The employer's deferred profit-sharing contribution will be allowed as an operating expense, as- it now is.
(b)	The employer's deferred profit-sharing contribution will not be subject to tax in the employee's hands unless and until he receives it.
(c)	The earnings of the trust fund must not be taxed in the hands of the trust.
(e) The terms of each deferred profit-sharing plan would be subject to initial and continuing approval by the Department of National Revenue, just as pension plans now are.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I enjoy speaking at this hour of night, though I have never done it before because of the character and ability of hon. members who stay here on Friday nights. I want to repeat what the Conservatives have said, with perhaps a slight addition. This is a bad budget. It is bad for the Conservatives. It is bad for the big people. Therefore it must be good for the little people. When the minister completed his budget I considered it to be a good election budget. Why shouldn't it be?
This budget is good for three reasons. It is good because of the way it has dealt with the past. It is good because of the way it "s dealing with the present. It is certainly good for the way it intends to deal with the future. What has it done for the past? I can remember when certain groups in Canada were predicting a depression after the second world war, just as one had occurred after the first world war. That depression has not started yet. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that there is no depression in sight, and that this country will have a population of 30 million before very long. The Leader of the Opposition does say some good things with which I agree. Because we are going to have no depression in the future, there is no reason to make a change.
This budget is good because of the way in which it has taken care of the war debt. I think the minister has tackled this problem very well. In the words of a heavy taxpayer who is known to me very well, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has not cut his taxes but he has cut the national debt. I think in doing that the minister
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor showed good sense. A reduction of $2-2 billion in the national debt represents a lot of money. I find it difficult to imagine how much a million dollars is because I have never had that much in my hands or in my possession, and I do not expect I ever shall. When it can be shown that $63 million is the amount of the reduction in our interest burden every year I think it will be realized that this is a good budget in the way it has dealt with the past.
An individual should pay his debts. Not long ago I was talking to a doctor who told me that he could retire to Florida if 40 per cent of the money owing him were paid. He agreed that a man should pay his debts if he could. Therefore a country should pay its debts if possible.
What effect has this paying off of the national debt had on others? It has had two effects. First of all, it lowered our debt and the interest charges thereon. Second, it advertised Canada all over the world, and I think you will admit that we have not enough people selling Canada today to the world. We are the greatest country on earth. Notwithstanding what has been said, we have lower tax bills than the United States, Great Britain, Australia or New Zealand. Canada is the greatest trading country for its size in the world. There is nothing like it, and I was not a bit surprised to observe the tense interest that was shown in the report made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Of course he did not polish it off with stories and incidents. He stuck to facts, and his speech will be long remembered.
Therefore I say that this is a good budget for everybody in the country. It is not a bad budget for the big man or the small man. There are those who say that some help has been given corporations, but who gets part of that help? Not all the money in corporations comes from rich people. You and I know that hundreds of people have small holdings in corporations. Who is it that gets the benefit? It is the man who makes the corporation live, the toiler, the artisan, the labourer. I was certainly greatly pleased to hear the hon. member who just sat down say, putting it in my own words, that the hope of labour is to share in profits. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) will forgive me for quoting him so often but I admire him in a way and some of the things he and his company have done for Fort William. The men now share in the profits in a way.
We have some business concerns in Fort William that do share the profits with their workers after their salaries are paid. They are a credit to the place. That is the cure

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor for strikes. I do not want to see strikes eliminated until something better is put in their place. Strikes have done some good and they have done some harm. They are like an operation on the human body. They are an eruption, and it takes a while to cure them. I am sorry to say that we have a strike in Fort William today that has not yet been settled. I refer to the carpenters' strike. Many of the contractors have settled with their men, but there is one contractor who has not settled yet. I do not know what his background is or why he has not settled. Perhaps 1 will know better tomorrow why the contractor for the Central Mortgage and Housing Company will not settle with the union. I expect he will have to settle with the union before very long; and I regret this difficulty very much.
I think the budget is a good budget in dealing with the past. I would say it is also a good budget in dealing with the present. It is a good budget for the common people in the present. My first point is the tax exemption for the ingredients that go into bread. Not very long ago I saw a picture put out by the bakers showing that they are trying to get the vitamins back into bread again. One medical expert wrote me and said that white bread is not worth eating because the vitamins have been taken out of it. Now the vitamins are going back into the bread again, and the baking companies are doing it. The ingredients that are to put back the vitamins in bread are to be tax exempt. Bread is eaten by everybody; therefore that is a good move at this time.
There are many people who say that the reduction in the tax on cigarettes does not amount to very much, but I notice that there have been some very favourable comments. This again is something that concerns everybody. It is not only the rich and wealthy who smoke cigarettes. If you go up to the cafeteria you will find people with a cup of coffee or a bottle of pop and a cigarette; and I know the cafeteria entertains the aristocracy of the House of Commons and the Senate. I know they all enjoy a cigarette, and they like them much more now because they can save 4 cents a package. I do not save anything because I know cigarettes would not do me any good. They would not make my head any clearer, my lungs any better, my heart any steadier or my stomach any more fit. Therefore I do not want cigarettes.
Another comment I should like to make having to do with the present concerns the deduction for medical expenses. This does not only concern rich people. It concerns


everybody, because at one time or another most people have a pain, and the increase in the allowable deduction for medical expenses is something that concerns the present. I remember hearing from many sources in the house remarks about the radio licence. It did not amount to very much before the budget was brought down, and now that it has been done away with I would say that it is a good thing because it touches so many people. I would say that the budget is a good budget for the present in its elimination of this nuisance tax.
Another tax change that I appreciated very .much more was the elimination of the tax on books and newsprint. I should like to have seen all taxes on books and newsprint removed. There should be no tax of any description on reading matter that is worth reading. There are those who have been telling us that the farmers are having a terrible time, that they are terribly hard up, that they were never so hard up. Perhaps they did not go so far as that but anyway, according to them, they are having a terrible time making ends meet. That is not my experience, but I do remember the time when I could have bought eggs for 10 cents a dozen 36 miles south of Fort William. However, I gave the lady 15 cents a dozen. They wanted to get cash.

The outlook is bright, and I would name a few of the things that make me feel that conditions will be better in the future.
First, we have entered a new age, the age of atomic energy. Nobody knows how far it is going in the future, but you have heard often in this house of the benefits that have come to those who are afflicted with cancer. When a man or woman had cancer it was considered almost hopeless; but we have now heard of so many cases that have been helped by the cobalt bomb.
Looking at the future, what will the St. Lawrence waterway do for us? We know that it will do something for the lakehead, and it will do a lot for Canada. It will do a lot for Ontario, and there is no doubt in our

Look at the fact that the government in the old land, the British government, sent the chancellor of the exchequer here to find out the best ways and places in which to invest British money. Why? Because there is no doubt about it that investment in Canada today is safe.
According to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) trade is going to extend to the south. It cannot help it. The markets are there, and if we have goods to sell it is up to Canada to advertise and sell those goods.
There is one other outstanding reason why I think the future is going to be great. While I am not a prophet, I would say that the war in Korea is not going to last many years. I think it will end; but there are some people who say that when it does end the bottom will drop out of everything. Well, the bottom did not drop out of everything after the second world war because the Minister of Trade and Commerce was able to manipulate and manage things with businessmen all over Canada so that instead of a depression industry picked up; and you all know what happened in Ontario and Quebec.
In my own way of looking at it you are not going to have peace on earth by preparation for war only. You will only have lasting peace when the people of Russia, China, Britain, Canada and the United States follow the teaching of the Prince of Peace and practise it in the -way I know some of you practise it.
There are one or two other things I would like to say. I congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, the former Speaker and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) on the greatly improved acoustics we now have in this chamber. It is a fine thing for the house, for the press gallery and for the public galleries, but there is one weakness in it. Why is it that I can hear a man in the far corner very well but I cannot even hear the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those who are close to me? I cannot hear him half as well as I could before. I heard him then distinctly enough, but I cannot hear him now. I understand that situation is going to be remedied, and if so it will be a fine thing.
I would like to see the Minister of Finance and the government do two things. I would like to see them grant pensions for the incapacitated men and women who cannot earn a dollar, people who are loved by their own fathers and mothers and other folks but who cannot earn money. It is one of the greatest needs in Canada today and whether I am in this house or whether I am not, I am

Then I think the means test should be removed in the case of pensions for the blind, because they are in a far worse state than men in this house who get old age pensions. Old age pensioners in the majority are not nearly as badly off as are the blind, and the means test for them should be removed.
Some of you might like to buy or build a home in Fort William, and there you will find bright prospects. I belonged to and was foreman of a fire brigade at one time, and I appreciate the services of a good fire brigade. In Fort William we have a brigade that is second to none. They have three-way radio and up-to-date equipment. The firemen are mostly young, sober, well trained and efficient. The result is that insurance rates in Fort William have dropped. Therefore if anyone thinks of retiring and coming to Fort William he will have protection of the right kind, and one of the finest water systems in the world.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for being so patient and not calling me to order.
