Mr. Speaker, this year again the workers of the Chicoutimi district will not benefit from any important reduction in the taxation burden.
The very slight reduction in income tax will really be felt only next year and even then it will not be very noticeable. The elimination of stamps on cheques and the deduction concerning dividends benefit mainly rich people and large business concerns.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) who, seemingly, endeavoured to please everyone apparently brought disappointment to many people.
We must regret that the government did not deem advisable to do more to protect the wage earner, the small wage earners, the little fellow, who have to face the problems of life; we regret that they refused to raise exemptions to $3,000 for married people and to $1,500 for single persons, as has been often requested.
We must also deplore the way the farmers are being neglected and forgotten. The wholesale price index of farm products has fallen by nearly 20 per cent, and that of machinery and labour has increased or has remained at a very high level.
The government should show more consideration for the working classes and be less concerned about big corporations. Agricultural and industrial workers deserve


special treatment and it must be remembered from time to time that on their own prosperity rests the prosperity of the whole nation.
As for the sympathy of the minister for the provincial authorities, deprived by him of their main source of revenue, it may show his good nature but, unfortunately, it does not change the situation.
The blunt fact is that out of every tax dollar paid by the citizen of Quebec, the government in Ottawa takes approximately 77 cents, the provincial treasury 13 cents, and the municipalities 10 cents.
Last December, I stated in this house that as a result of the fiscal agreements concluded between the other provinces and the central government, Quebec now found itself isolated. I added that Quebec should not be blamed for this state of affairs, but that the responsible party was the Ottawa government who, with the millions of dollars exacted from the French Canadians, were now proceeding to offer to buy their rights from them.
But the present day French Canadians, fortunately, just as those of bygone, days, are much too proud to be the servants of Ottawa and to live on its subsidies. The part of beggars in confederation is not made for us.
The struggle for the last remnants of provincial autonomy, which is so gallantly being waged by the premier of Quebec, is the very same struggle begun by the great Liberal leaders of our race: Laurier, Mercier, Gouin and Taschereau.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in 1883:
I repeat: every time a particular province is divested in this parliament (Ottawa) of a right it exercises, insignificant though it may be, it is one more step towards legislative union.
On November 24, 1871, he said:
It is an historic fact that the federative system was adopted solely in order to maintain Quebec in its exceptional and unique position on the American continent.
The interference, the impingement of the Ottawa government in matters coming under the jurisdiction of the provinces is not of recent origin. We must admit, however, that this intrusion has increased in the course of the last few years, to such an extent that it has now become a very acute problem. We are therefore justified in protesting against the violations of the clauses of the B.N.A. Act by the federal authorities, and in denouncing the systematic infringements of the promoters of centralization in spheres which concern the provinces only. Allow me to quote, in support of these arguments, a few statements showing the merits of our claims and the soundness of our fears.

Mr. Mercier, in a speech he made before the legislative assembly on April 7, 1884, said:
I have the honour to move that an address be presented to His Honour the Lieutenant Governor asking him to kindly transmit to His Excellency the Governor General the following resolutions:
1.	That the British North America Act, 1867, was intended by its authors to sanction the autonomy of the provinces of the confederation, and that this act has definitely settled the respective powers of the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures;
2.	That the frequent encroachments of the federal parliament upon the prerogatives of the provinces are a constant menace for the provinces; and that this house, rightly alarmed at such encroachments, believes it is duty bound to express emphatically its resolve to uphold the provincial rights and to proclaim loudly the autonomy which it enjoys and which has been sanctioned by the federal act.
When confronted with such dangers as those which threaten us at present, and when faced with a plot directed against the privileges and the independence of the provinces, the party man vanishes, to be replaced by the citizen, who sets the interests of his province above his personal success and for whom his country is more important than his party.
The provinces existed before the dominion became an entity; it is the provinces who granted the dominion its powers. The provinces had responsible government in 1867; they had their legislature, their laws and that measure of autonomy which a colony is allowed. In the interest of the country as a whole, the provinces delegated part of their powers; that part they did not delegate, they withheld and it is still theirs. Within the sphere of their prerogatives, they exercise sovereign power and any infringement upon this sovereignty is a breach of the federal pact.
"Legislative powers are rather ill-defined in the federal act, and the vagueness in the terms of sections 91 and 92 is causing a good many difficulties. However, as far as I am concerned, I am rather inclined,-
says Mr. Mercier further,
-to accept the doctrines set forth in this respect by the Hon. T. J. J. Loranger. They are clear and satisfactory. I shall quote them, as they are found on pages XXV and XXVI of the first report of the commission for the revision of provincial statutes:
1.	The confederation of the British provinces was the result of a pact made by the provinces and the imperial parliament, which when enacting the North America Act, only ratified it.
2.	The provinces entered into the federal union with their corporative identity, their former constitutions and all their legislative powers, some of which they agreed to surrender to the federal parliament, to be used in their common interest for general purposes, while keeping the remainder to be exercised by their legislators, acting within their provincial sphere, and according to their former constitution subject to certain changes in form established by the federal pact.
3.	Far from having been granted to them by the federal government, the powers of the provinces which have been withheld from this government are the remainder of their former powers and far from having been set up by this government the federal power proceeds from their association and agreement and has been created by them.
4.	Parliament has no other legislative powers than those which the provinces have vested in it and which are recognized by section 91 of the
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon British North America Act which granted it only the powers outlined therein or those of a similar nature, ejusdem generis.
5.	Apart from the powers conferred under section 91 and section 92, the legislatures have legislative jurisdiction extending to all matters of local or private interest; all cases not included fall under the jurisdiction of the provinces when they concern the local or private interests of a single province or of a few provinces only. Matters which concern all the provinces come within the jurisdiction of parliament.
6.	When it is not clear whether a matter concerns all or only a few of the provinces, that is whether such a matter is of national or local interest, such doubt must be solved in favour of the provinces who kept all the powers not conferred on parliament.
7.	In their respective fields of jurisdiction, there is no superiority of parliament over the provinces, and, although subject to imperial sovereignty, those provinces are sovereign in their own field and are absolutely equal.
That is definitely what the fathers of confederation had in mind, and I quote the words of some of them: Matters of general interest will be under the control of the central or federal parliament, as was established at the Quebec conference, but all matters of local interest, everything which relates to the affairs and rights of the different sections of our confederation will remain under the control of the local legislatures. (Sir Hector Langevin)
Local legislatures will hold control over all local undertakings; that is an important point and one of the main advantages of the existence of a federal union and of local parliaments, because in that way each province will have the power and the means to develop its own resources and to work unfettered towards its individual progress. (Sir John A. Macdonald)
Nobody can hold any doubt as to the fact that our autonomy is guaranteed by the constitution; everybody will admit, however, that our autonomy is threatened by our central government.
One need but look at the present situation to be convinced that systematic efforts are being made in high places to deprive the provinces of their rights.
The province of Quebec has been the cradle of our great country. Will that province, which during a memorable period of our history brought forth those heroes who gave their lives on the scaffold in order to defend our political rights and our national freedom, bear without flinching the shameful spoliations of which it is the victim?
Mr. Alexandre Taschereau, Sir Lamer Gouin's successor-

-upheld the same views on autonomy. The federal government was offering subsidies in exchange of rights which it purported to monopolize. Alexandre Taschereau, the new premier, made a very formal declaration of principle when he addressed the Quebec Reform Club on November 15, 1920. Mr. Ernest Lapointe supported him in these words:
As the honourable premier said a few minutes ago, Ottawa is more or less trying to buy us. Many citizens in this province do not seem to protest loudly enough against such a trap. We, in the province of Quebec, must not lose hold of even a small portion of our autonomy and our rights.

speechtext:
November 15, 1920, at the Quebec Reform Club, a club my hon. friend knows well.
Alexandre Taschereau resisted the King government, although it was of the same political colour, but he sided with the Ontario government even though it was Conservative. Ferguson, the premier of Ontario, maintained regulation XVII and was said to be ill-disposed towards French Canadians. Nevertheless, Taschereau found it permissible and even necessary to side with Ferguson and later with Henry, just as Merrier had sided with Mowat and as Gouin had sided with Whitney, for the defence of provincial autonomy.
The premiers who have guided the destinies of my province since confederation were not the only ones to foresee the danger of centralization. The premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Angus L. Macdonald, made in 1947, before the members of the Halifax junior board of trade, a statement which should be underlined. To appraise fully his statement, it must be recalled that Mr. Macdonald, who is now the Liberal premier of his province, is a former member of the Mackenzie King federal cabinet.
(Text):
Can anyone deny that, if most of the revenues which the provinces are to enjoy are to be paid to them by the dominion, the time may not come- indeed, it is not likely that the time is sure to come-when the dominion will begin to say what use the provinces shall make of these revenues? When that day comes, there will be an end to provincial autonomy. This is not a matter of the provinces endeavouring to magnify their own importance. It is a case of believing that whatever the conditions may be in Canada 50 to 100 years hence, the time has not yet come when it is in the interest of the people of this country to dispense with provincial governments.
If they are to continue, they must be given a certain measure of freedom. They must be given certain taxation fields which are theirs and theirs alone. I disagree here with statements made by dominion authorities to the effect that there is nothing in their proposals to interfere with provincial autonomy.
We are told by them that financial independence for the provinces means provincial autonomy. But is it independence for the provinces when so much of their revenue is to come from Ottawa? Furthermore, is it exclusively for the dominion to say what is or is not genuine provincial autonomy? Are the provinces to have no voice in the matter?
(Translation):
And, on September 9, 1948, at the annual dinner of the Canadian Good Roads Association in Digby, the same Mr. Macdonald said: (Text):
And then we have problems of jurisdiction as between the dominion and the provinces. We live here under a federal system, as they do in the


United States. We are not a unitary state, we are not a single state with a single government, as is the case of Great Britain. We are a federation, and we are that by our own choice, made in 1867. There were people at that time of confederation who would have liked to see the unitary system of government adopted in Canada, one government for all of Canada-one central government. The idea had to be abandoned and what we have in Canada today is not one government but ten governments (now eleven). We have the federal or central government at Ottawa dealing with certain matters that are definitely assigned to it by our constitution-such great matters as defence, railways, postal services, trade and commerce are confined to the central government. But I would like this to be remembered-we have nine provincial governments (now ten) in Canada, also dealing with matters that are assigned to them by the constitution, and some of these are of great importance. They are education, property and civil rights, public welfare and charities, the construction of roads and many other things that touch people intimately and all matters of provincial government concern. It is a mistake to say that this country is governed entirely from Ottawa. It is governed in some respects from there, in others from the provincial capitals.
There are people in Canada today who say that federalism is out of date and that things would be simpler if we had one government for the entire country.
To them I say this-whatever conditions may be 100 years from now in Canada, my judgment is that this country, at this time, is not ready for the unitary system. The provinces were here before the Dominion of Canada. The provinces created the Dominion of Canada, and in a country of this size, with its various races, its differences of language, its varying economic and geographic conditions, it seems to me that only by a true federation can the unity of the country be maintained.
(Translation):
If autonomy is valuable to each of the provinces of our kingdom, to ours it is sacred. We must guard against those whom the magazine Relations called, in its issue of September, 1946, the unrepentant centralizers:
There are unrepentant centralizers, anxious to extend more and more the powers of the federal government over every field, at the expense of the provinces. They miss no opportunity to promote their cause, being well versed in the art of multiplying facts and measures favourable to their objective. They are, on the other hand, in an admirable position to do it. Consequently, the provinces demand that their taxation rights, surrendered to Ottawa for the duration of the war, be handed back to them: the latter refuses, pretexting liabilities assumed with full knowledge of the facts, and which were bound to mobilize all the resources of the country, including those of the provinces. In like manner, the government on two occasions put a motion through to amend the constitution, without asking the consent of the provinces which were parties to the pact of 1867, or without even consulting them.
The very same centralizing spirit leads to the monopoly of the air waves through the agency of the C.B.C. This agency is monopolizing more and more channels and strangling private broadcasting. The government pays no heed to the justified complaints of public opinion and of provincial governments. And how many attempts there have been to interfere even in education, that field which is so particularly reserved to the provinces! Though

there is no open violation of provincial rights, whose interpretation is narrowed down as much as possible, there is a constant attempt to praise the advantage of federal subsidies, the necessity of action from Ottawa so that every Canadian may receive the same advantages as far as education is concerned, to unify and fortify Canadian spirit. There are more and more attempts made all the time to bring the physical training of our youth under federal jurisdiction, to train young people of all ages through cadet corps maintained even after the war, through mass education by the national film board.
Some measures, acceptable intrinsically, carry about them an aura of suspicion because of the centralizing tendencies of the people in Ottawa. For instance the Foreign Exchange Control Act might well become an instrument of political pressure and vexation against the provinces which have to obtain permission from the federal government before negotiating a loan on foreign markets.
Shall we have to repeat it again? What the French Canadians are defending, against the centralizers in particular, is not conquered territories or political or financial ambitions. It is values which belong to them by all rights, religious and cultural values, which make up the precious heritage of French Canada. It is well known that "the strength which gives drive and unity to French Canadian life" is "the Roman Catholic religion", to use the words of a shrewd observer of the French Canadian soul. These values are threatened by enemies from the outside-not to mention the ones inside, who are perhaps even more dangerous-whose plans would benefit from centralization.
Moreover, in defending their rights and heritage, the French Canadians have reason to believe that they are working in the best interests of Canada as a whole. If this is nationalism carried to extremes, we admit our guilt without repentance. History will show some day that the real enemies of a unified and prosperous Canada were not the French Canadians.
The Rural Co-operator on March 8, 1949, wrote:
(Text):
The fear of the people of Quebec that the dominion parliament might become too powerful and rub out the minority rights of French-speaking Canadians is understandable. French language Canadians are in a minority in the dominion parliament, but they are in a majority in the Quebec legislature. Therefore they rely on the provincial legislature to protect their rights of language.
(Translation):
George Brown, Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, in turn, have stated:
-that without the consent of Lower Canada, confederation could not have taken place.
I cannot believe that the authors of the pact of 1867 wanted to deceive us; I maintain that they had no intention of destroying the provincial governments, and that the federal government sets this pact of honour at defiance when it exacts from the people, as it does today, nearly 80 per cent of all taxes.
Not only did the fathers of confederation intend that direct taxation should belong only to the provincial administrations, but they said so and made promises to that effect.
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon Alexander Galt, minister of finance at the time of the Cartier-Macdonald government, noted that the fiscal problem had been solved-
-by transferring to the federal government all major income sources, by placing at its disposal, with only one exception, that of direct taxation, all the means through which the industry of the people can be made to contribute to the needs of the state. As a matter of fact (I quote Le Devoir of May 4, 1946), the parliamentary debates of 1867 show without a shadow of doubt that neither the federal government nor the provinces wanted direct taxation; it was, in effect, extremely unpopular and it was left to the provinces, under the pretence that it would enable them to curb their expenditures wisely.
Let us give back to the provinces the revenue sources arising from direct taxation; Quebec will then no longer need to depend on Ottawa's charities which, in fact, are but mere restitutions.
It is what we are asking for, it is the very thing which is demanded by an overwhelming majority of the people of Quebec. The chamber of commerce recently submitted a brief which shows how dangerous the dominion government's centralizing policy may be; that brief expresses the opinion of the people of my province, and in its issue of November 28, 1952, the Montreal Gazette stated:
(Text):
Anyone who attempts to diminish the fears in this province about centralization would do well to remember this delegation and its memorandum. La Chambre de Commerce de la Province de Quebec was not playing politics. It was expressing, with anxiety, Quebec's point of view.
It has been one of the chief aims of Canadian statesmanship in times past to give that point of view the fullest understanding. Quebec's anxiety on this issue should now be a matter of concern for all Canada, just because it is a matter of such concern for Quebec.
Anyone who attempts to brush the whole matter aside as "mere politics" had best remember that it is the memorandum of the chambre de commerce that says: Never in the history of the Canadian confederation have our rights to provincial autonomy been in such serious danger.
When Premier Duplessis expresses such views he is taking a stand that is, quite evidently, broader than party. He is speaking for Quebec.
(Translation):
This appetite, this lust for centralization on the part of the federal government is nothing new, as I recalled a few moments ago, but it can only grow if we recall also that the Prime Minister has championed, in. this house, the case of the central power, when we know that he was the legal adviser of the Rowell-Sirois commission whose recommendations, too rigorous, in the view of the Minister of Finance himself, implied the renunciation by the provinces of part of their autonomy.

Today then, more than ever, we must be alert. For us, particularly, who want no part of a legislative union and who do not want to become the wards of Ottawa, our duty is to be alert. We must do this if we are to pass on without change the religious, cultural and national heritage we have received from our ancestors. The inroads made into provincial autonomy should be sealed off and our rights restored in all their integrity. That is the price of our survival as French Canadians.
The subsidies and grants which we are offered in exchange for privileges given us by the constitution of our country conceal, under attractive guise, traps designed to weld the chains of our servitude and dependence. May Providence help us refuse them always categorically.

Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with this debate on the budget on Monday we will move the second reading of Bill No. 107, to amend the Post Office Act, so we may refer it to the select committee which has been set up to consider it. There was quite a lengthy debate at the resolution stage and we hope that second reading will be agreed to without too many speeches. We think that when it comes back to the house hon. members will have more details and will thus be in better position to discuss it.
I mentioned this procedure to hon. members of the three opposition parties and although they did not agree because their leaders were not present, the suggestion seemed to appeal to them. We would not want to interrupt the budget debate for too long and we hope we can send this bill to the committee.
On motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) the house adjourned at 9.55 p.m.
